Chrono Trigger

A byte-exact decompilation of the 1995 classic, one matched routine at a time

Welcome to ChronoRET, a byte-exact matching decompilation of Chrono Trigger (SNES, US 1.0).

The goal is hand-labeled 65816 assembly that assembles back to a ROM that is bit-for-bit identical to the original 1995 cartridge. Every matched function is verified with make diff before it is committed.

This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Square or Square Enix in any way.

Overall: 28,030 bytes matched — ~7.8% of all game code (359,278 bytes), ~31.56% of Bank $C0 (61,779 bytes), ~12.61% of Bank $C1 (63,904 bytes). The 4 MB ROM is mostly graphics and music data; only ~359 KB is executable 65816 code.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Each function goes through four steps before it is marked matched:

  1. Disassemble — tools/disasm.py traces execution from a known entry point, tracking M/X flag state to decode operand widths correctly.
  2. Annotate — Labels, equates, and inline comments added by hand.
  3. Assemble — asar rebuilds the function; known assembler quirks (BRL offsets, STA addressing) are worked around explicitly.
  4. Verify — make diff compares the assembled output byte-for-byte against the original ROM. Only a clean diff gets committed.

docs.title: Engine Architecture
docs.text: A high-level map of the Chrono Trigger SNES engine as recovered from matched code. Everything here is verified — it comes from byte-exact matched routines, not guesswork.

docs.title: Boot sequence
docs.text:
Power-on / RESET vector ($00:FF00)
  └─ Reset (7 bytes)
       SEI / CLC / XCE        native mode on
       JML MainInit            jump to bank $FD

$FD:C000 — MainInit (215 bytes)
  ├─ CPU: SEI, native mode, DP=0, DB=0, SP=$01FF
  ├─ PPU: forced blank, zero all PPU registers
  ├─ APU: boot SPC700 with silent init payload
  ├─ WRAM: DMA zero-fill all 128KB via ClearRAMDMA stub address
  └─ JML GameLoop              jump to bank $C0

docs.title: Game loop
docs.text:
$C0:000E — GameLoop (one-shot startup)
  ├─ JSR ClearRAMDMA ($C0:2DF1)   zero-fill WRAM via DMA
  ├─ JSR InstallNMI ($C0:0B64)    write JML $C0:EA63 → $7E:0500
  ├─ JSR InstallIRQ ($C0:0B75)    write JML $C0:ECCC → $7E:0504
  └─ falls into GameLoop_Main

$C0:005D — GameLoop_Main (per-mode outer loop)
  ├─ JSR FrameStateInit ($C0:0B86) reset per-frame state
  ├─ LDA/STA mode dispatch on $0100
  ├─ enters GameLoop_FrameBody
  └─ loops back

$C0:0097 — GameLoop_FrameBody (tight per-frame inner loop)
  ├─ JSR $C0:881E    (unknown — possibly DMA trigger)
  ├─ JSR Sub_0C76    (door/switch tile-opening dispatch + scene transition gate)
  ├─ JSR Sub_18D9    (screen-transition gate: fade, reinit, scene context save/restore)
  ├─ JSR $C0:1AAC    (unknown)
  ├─ JSL $C0:1F87    (cross-bank — possibly audio)
  ├─ JSL $C0:21E1
  ├─ JSL $C0:274D
  └─ BRL → VBlankHandler / loops

docs.title: VBlank handler
docs.text:
$C0:00BF — VBlankHandler (per-NMI, each frame)
  ├─ JSR $C0:881E    (shared with frame loop)
  ├─ audio/DMA work
  └─ BRL PostVBlank  (tail call — no RTS; returns to VBlankHandler's caller)

$C0:00DE — VBlankHandlerShort (minimal path, no audio)
  └─ RTS

$C0:B271 — PostVBlank (152 bytes, matched)
  ├─ Reset OAM hardware DMA channel registers
  ├─ Walk sprite descriptor table ($7E:0E00, 63 entries × 2 bytes)
  │    for each active entry: JSR Sub_B309 (build OAM buffer slot)
  │    follow chain links until chain byte < 0 (end marker)
  ├─ Fill unused OAM slots with Y=$E0 (off-screen)
  └─ RTS

$C0:B309 — Sub_B309 (1016 bytes, matched)
  ├─ JSR Sub_B701 → BCC skip  (gate: skip if sprite not ready)
  ├─ LDX $6D / LDA $1201,X / AND #$03 → sprite type dispatch (0/1/2/3+)
  │
  ├─ Each type path:
  │    PHD / REP #$20 / LDA #$2100 / TCD / SEP #$20   (DP=$2100 trick)
  │    LDA $0F80,X / AND #$0C → OAM range dispatch (bits 2-3)
  │
  ├─ Range dispatch (per type, 3 sub-paths):
  │    Range 1 (bits 2-3 = 00): OAM write-head at $0181, WRAM dest at $01DB
  │    Range 2 (bit 2 set):     OAM write-head at $0185, WRAM dest at $01DD
  │    Range 3 (bit 3 only):    OAM write-head at $0189, WRAM dest at $01DF
  │
  ├─ OAM write per type (from bank $7F staging buffer → OAM slot):
  │    type 0: 1 byte  (LDA.l $7F4F00,X → STX $0181 range → STA.w $0000,X)
  │    type 1: 2 bytes (LDA.l $7F4F01,X / PHA / LDA.l $7F4F00,X → write pair)
  │    type 2: 3 bytes (LDA.l $7F4B40,X / PHA / $7F4F01,X / PHA / $7F4F00,X)
  │    type 3+: 6 bytes (5×PHA + 1 in A, from $7F4F81/$7F4F80/$7F4B41/$7F4B40/$7F4F01/$7F4F00)
  │
  ├─ WRAM dest advance (per type):
  │    LDX $01DB / STX $81 (→ WMADDL=$2181 via DP=$2100 trick)
  │    REP #$20 / LDA $01DB / CLC / ADC #$0010 (or $20/$30/$60) / STA $01DB
  │
  ├─ Shared gfx+palette loop (per type, all 3 ranges converge here):
  │    LDA $1700,X → TAX  (sprite gfx index, 16-bit)
  │    LDA #$04 (or $08/$0C/$18) → STA $01C9  (palette loop counter)
  │    loop: LDA.l $7F4BC0,X / STA $80 (WMDATA via DP trick) ×4 per iter
  │           REP #$20 / TXA / CLC / ADC #$0008 / TAX / SEP #$20
  │           DEC $01C9 / BNE loop
  │
  └─ PLD / RTS

$C0:B701 — Sub_B701 (135 bytes, matched)
  (see below)

docs.title: Per-frame reset
docs.text:
$C0:0B86 — FrameStateInit (240 bytes, matched)
  ├─ Save sprite registers ($00/$02/$04) → ($0A/$0C/$0E)
  ├─ STZ ~25 per-frame flags ($10, $11, $17, $18, $38, etc.)
  ├─ Set defaults: sprite Y=$E0, OAM write-head limits
  │    $7D=$0900 / $7F=$0770 / $7B=$08A0
  ├─ Set palette defaults: $B1/$B4/$B7/$BA=$E4
  ├─ REP #$20 → 16-bit A section:
  │    STZ $2B / STZ $0150 / STZ $58
  │    LDA.l $E4FFE0/$E2/$E4/$E6 → STA $AF/$B2/$B5/$B8  (ROM seeds)
  │    STA.l $7E:2000 = 0
  ├─ SEP #$20 → 8-bit A:
  │    STA #$80 → $97/$99/$9B/$8D/$8E/$8F/$91/$90/$92/$93
  │    LDA.l $7E:2980/$81/$82 → $94/$95/$96  (WRAM color vars)
  │    STA $EB=$AE=$80 / $55=$01 / $FC=$53 / $FB=$65 / $FA=$45
  │    STA.l $7E:2989 = 0
  │    STA $0BD9/$0BDA/$0BDB/$0BE9 = 0
  │    LDA $0400 → STA $F8    (scene entry point)
  └─ RTS

docs.title: RAM-resident handlers
docs.text:
NMI and IRQ handlers live in WRAM, installed at boot:

WRAM addr Installed by Target Purpose $7E:0500 InstallNMI JML $C0:EA63 Real NMI handler (unmatched) $7E:0504 InstallIRQ JML $C0:ECCC Real IRQ handler (unmatched)

This pattern allows the game to swap handlers at runtime without patching ROM.

docs.title: Key data structures
docs.text:
Sprite descriptor table ($7E:0E00, 63 entries × 2 bytes): - Byte 0: sprite type index (negative = inactive slot) - Byte 1: chain link (index of next sprite in chain, negative = end) - PostVBlank walks this table each frame to build the OAM buffer

OAM buffer ranges (in WRAM): - Range 1: $7B–$08A0 (pointer stored at $7B) - Range 2: $7D–$0900 (pointer stored at $7D) - Range 3: $7F–$0770 (pointer stored at $7F) - Filled with Y=$E0 for unused slots to hide off-screen

Per-frame dp variables (DP=$0100 in game loop):

dp WRAM Width Contents $00 $0100 16-bit Active sprite X position $02 $0102 16-bit Active sprite Y position $04 $0104 8-bit Active sprite attribute $0A $010A 16-bit Saved previous-frame sprite X $0C $010C 16-bit Saved previous-frame sprite Y $0E $010E 8-bit Saved previous-frame attribute $17 $0117 8-bit Per-frame flag (branch key in $C0:0C76) $18 $0118 8-bit Per-frame flags (bits 2/8 tested for JSR targets) $19 $0119 8-bit Scene transition counter $6D $016D 16-bit Current sprite descriptor index (PostVBlank loop var) $97 $0197 8-bit Palette seed index (default $80) $F8 $01F8 8-bit Scene entry point (from $0400)

docs.title: Sprite render/init cluster
docs.text:
Calls from Sub_B309 → Sub_B701 → per-type init and render routines:

Sub_B701 type 0:
  positive state → JSR Sub_B8CA (init helper 1) → JSR Sub_E9E2 (init helper 2)
  negative state → JSR Sub_B788 (renderer)

Sub_B701 type 1:
  positive high-state → JSR Sub_BCDC (high-state init) → JSR Sub_E9FF (init pass 2)
  negative low-state  → JSR Sub_BA65 (low-state init)

Sub_B701 types 2/3+:
  low-state (neg) → JSR Sub_BFF2 (12-tile low-state init; BMI-split pos path; BCS/BPL type-3+ path)
  high-state (pos) → JSR Sub_C2BF (12-tile high-state init; BPL/CMP/BCS pos path, no BMI-split; raw→staging copies)

Sub_B701 type 3+:
  BRL Sub_C73A (renderer, 6-tile)
  Sub_C73A calls Sub_C6E7 ×6 (X-pos helper, 4 tiles each)

docs.title: Y-dispatch 3-way patterns — NOT uniform across routines
docs.text:
All matched routines with Y-clamp logic share the same logical structure — dispatch on $C6 first, then on the sign of $C5 — but use different branch mnemonics and clamp conditions in each path. Do not assume a pattern from one routine applies to another. Verify each branch byte explicitly.

Routine C6=0 dispatch (on C5) C6≠0 clamp logic C6=0 neg clamp C6=0 pos clamp Tiles Sub_B788 BPL → positive BCS→clamp, BMI→clamp BPL+4/BCS+2 BPL+4/BCS+2 8 Sub_B8CA BPL → positive BCC→clamp, CMP/BCS→store BCC+6/BCC+2 BPL+6/BCS+2 8 Sub_C73A BMI → no-clamp BCS→clamp, BPL→store BPL+2/BCS+2 BPL+2/BCS+2 24 Sub_BA65 BPL → positive BCC→$E0, CMP/BCS→store CMP/BCC→store BMI-split: BPL/CMP/BCS 8 Sub_BCDC BMI → negative BCC→clamp, CMP/BCS→store CMP/BCC→store BPL/CMP/BCS (no BMI-split) 8 Sub_BFF2 BMI → negative BCS/BPL clamp (new variant) direct add, no clamp BMI-split: BPL/CMP/BCS 12 Sub_C2BF BMI → negative BCS/BPL clamp (same as BFF2) raw copy + direct add raw copy + BPL/CMP/BCS (no BMI-split) 12

The BPL/BMI switch on C5 is especially counterintuitive: Sub_B788, Sub_B8CA, and Sub_BA65 use BPL to reach the positive (C5<$80) path, while Sub_C73A, Sub_BCDC, and Sub_BFF2 use BMI to reach the negative (C5≥$80) path. Same logical signal, opposite dispatch direction.

Sub_BFF2 and Sub_C2BF together confirm two patterns:

  1. BMI-split tracks the low-state family — now confirmed across both type pairs. Sub_BFF2's positive path (low-state, types 2/3+) uses the BMI-split (BPL → skip, CMP #$E0, BCS → skip, else LDA #$E0) — same as Sub_BA65 (low-state, type 1). Sub_C2BF's positive path (high-state, types 2/3+) uses NO BMI-split, reading raw table ($4804,X → $4BC4,X) before applying BPL/CMP/BCS — same as Sub_BCDC (high-state, type 1). The correlation holds across TWO type pairs:
  2. High-state (Sub_BCDC type 1, Sub_C2BF types 2/3+): no BMI-split, raw table copy in Y path

  3. Low-state (Sub_BA65 type 1, Sub_BFF2 types 2/3+): BMI-split, reads staging Y directly

  4. BCS/BPL clamp ordering is shared between low-state and high-state C6≠0 paths. Sub_C2BF's C6≠0 path uses BCS → #$E0 / BPL → keep (carry first, sign second), identical to Sub_BFF2's C6≠0 path. This ordering is distinct from the earlier routines (Sub_BCDC, Sub_B8CA) which used BCC→clamp / CMP #$E0 / BCS→store. There are now three distinct carry/sign clamp orderings across the matched set.

docs.title: disasm.py — M-flag linear-decoder trap at loop-exit branches
docs.text:
Symptom: the decoder generates wrong M-state (and thus wrong instruction widths) for code immediately after a conditional branch that exits a loop containing REP #$20.

Root cause: when a BEQ/BPL/etc. exits a loop, the decoder queues the branch target (correct state) but continues linearly through the loop-continuation code. If that code contains REP #$20, the decoder's running M-flag becomes 0. When the linear scan then reaches the branch target address, it visits it with M=0 instead of M=1, and the queued correct-state entry is skipped (already-visited check).

Affected code: any loop where SEP #$20 is in the body but REP #$20 appears in the loop-continuation tail before the back-branch. Hit in Sub_C73A (sessions 11) and Sub_B8CA (session 12).

Fix (tools/disasm.py, branch handling): instead of falling through linearly after a conditional branch, terminate the linear scan and queue the fall-through as a separate work item. Both the branch-taken and fall-through paths then start from the correct M-state captured at the branch point, with neither able to contaminate the other.

Implication for manual decoding: if using an un-patched disasm.py output near a loop exit, manually re-derive M-state from the actual execution entry rather than trusting the disassembler's annotation. The error is always at the branch target of a BEQ/BPL that exits a loop, and the symptom is an immediate-mode instruction being decoded at double width.

docs.title: Staging buffer layout ($7F:4BXX)
docs.text:
8-byte stride per tile. For gfx_index-relative addressing (X = gfx_index):

X offset Width Written by Contents +$00 ($4BC0,X) 8-bit Sub_B788, Sub_B8CA, Sub_C6E7 Tile X low byte +$01 ($4BC1,X) 8-bit Sub_B788, Sub_B8CA, Sub_C73A Tile Y position (clamped) +$02 ($4BC2,X) 16-bit Sub_B788, Sub_B8CA Raw X offset (copy from $4802,X) +$04 ($4BC4,X) 8-bit Sub_B8CA Raw Y source (copy from $4804,X) +$06 ($4BC6,X) 16-bit Sub_B8CA Extra 16-bit field (copy from $4806,X)

docs.title: Sprite System Overview
docs.text:
The sprite subsystem is a fully matched, self-contained cluster spanning fourteen routines across two address ranges in bank $C0 ($B271–$C989 and $E9E2–$EA41). Every callee within the cluster is now matched; the cluster has no external call targets except matched helpers.

Entry point and frame trigger. Every frame, VBlankHandler tail-calls PostVBlank ($C0:B271). PostVBlank resets the OAM DMA channel registers, then walks the sprite descriptor table at $7E:0E00 (63 entries, 2 bytes each). For each active entry it calls Sub_B309 ($C0:B309), following chain-link bytes to handle multi-sprite objects, then fills any remaining OAM slots with Y=$E0 to park them off-screen.

Render dispatch (Sub_B309). Sub_B309 is the main per-sprite entry. It first calls Sub_B701 as a gate: if the gate sets carry, the sprite is not ready and Sub_B309 returns immediately. If the gate clears carry, Sub_B309 reads the sprite type from $7E:1201,X (bits 0–1: type 0/1/2/3+), then reads range selection bits (bits 2–3 of $7F:0F80,X) to pick one of three OAM write-heads ($0181/$0185/$0189) and WRAM destinations ($01DB/$01DD/$01DF). It uses the DP=$2100 trick (PHD/LDA #$2100/TCD) to alias PPU registers into the direct page. After writing the OAM position bytes from the $7F:4F00 staging buffer, it iterates the palette copy loop (4/8/12/24 iterations depending on type), reading from $7F:4BC0 into WMDATA ($2180 via DP trick).

State gate (Sub_B701). Sub_B701 dispatches on sprite type and reads the state byte at $7E:1B00,X. State zero means inactive (carry set, skip). A positive state below the per-type threshold means partially initialised (carry set, skip). A positive state at or above the threshold triggers the high-state init path. A negative state (bit 7 set, bits 0–6 non-zero) triggers the low-state init path. A state of exactly $80 means fully initialised and triggers rendering.

Init helpers — high state and low state. The distinction is the most important structural insight in the cluster. High-state init reads raw animation data from ROM/WRAM tables and copies it into the $7F:4B00 staging buffer before applying Y clamping. Low-state init reads Y data directly from the staging buffer that the previous high-state pass already populated. This produces different clamp code in each family.

For types 0: Sub_B8CA handles init (high-state only; type 0 has no separate low-state init path — Sub_B788 is its renderer). For type 1: Sub_BCDC is high-state init (raw table → staging, BPL/CMP/BCS positive path, no BMI-split); Sub_BA65 is low-state init (reads staging, BMI-split on positive path). For types 2/3+: Sub_C2BF is high-state init (same BPL/CMP/BCS pattern as BCDC, no BMI-split); Sub_BFF2 is low-state init (BMI-split, identical pattern to BA65). The BMI-split thus tracks exactly with the low-state family across both type pairs, and its absence tracks with the high-state family.

Pass 2 init (mark-and-exit). After each init helper runs, Sub_B701 calls a pass-2 helper to record the sprite's slot in the $7E:0BC0 entity table. Sub_E9E2 handles type 0 (4-entry search, marks 1 byte). Sub_E9FF handles type 1 (3-entry search, marks 2 bytes: $0BC0,X and $0BC1,X). Sub_EA1F handles types 2/3+ (2-entry search, marks 3 bytes: $0BC0,X, $0BC1,X, $0BC2,X). The pattern is consistent: the number of OAM slots a type uses equals the number of table bytes marked.

Renderers. Sub_B788 is the type 0 renderer (8-bit sprites, single OAM entry). Sub_C73A is the type 3+ renderer (6-tile sprites, 24 OAM entries); it calls Sub_C6E7 six times, once per tile group, to pack X-position overflow bits into the OAM attribute byte. Types 1 and 2 do not have separate renderer routines in the matched cluster; their render path is served by Sub_B309's direct OAM write.

Y-clamp ordering summary. Three distinct branch orderings appear. Type 3+ (Sub_C73A) uses BCS/BPL: carry first, sign second, because large tile X coordinates enter the clamp path with carry already set. High-state init routines (Sub_BCDC, Sub_C2BF) use BPL/CMP/BCS on the positive path: sign first, then compare against $E0, then carry — no BMI-split because the raw table value is always bounded. Low-state init routines (Sub_BA65, Sub_BFF2) add a BMI-split on the positive path: BPL skips the clamp check entirely for small positive Y values, because the staging buffer can hold values that the high-state pass already bounded, but a second clamp pass may still encounter borderline cases where an intermediate BMI branch saves work.

docs.title: Mode handler cluster ($C0:0D78–$16DB) — door/switch tile-opening dispatch
docs.text:
Five mode-specific scroll-map update handlers live in a contiguous block starting at $C0:0D78 and ending at $C0:16DB (just before the default handler at $16DC). These handlers implement the tile-opening animation for doors and interactive switches on the map: each frame, Sub_0C76 dispatches to the appropriate handler based on the current animation mode, the handler advances the $7E:3000 layer-state table, computes VRAM tilemap write indices corner-by-corner, and triggers an SPC audio cue. All five handlers share a two-phase structure:

Phase 1 — Mode-table prologue. Increments selected entries in the $7E:3000 layer-state table using LDA.l $7E3000,X / INC A / STA.l $7E3000,X. The number of entries updated scales with the handler: E6=2, EC=4, EE=4, FA=6, FC=6. All but E6 include at least one REP #$20; TXA; SEC; SBC #$0100; TAX; SEP #$20 block to index $100 rows back in the table. The prologue ends with JSR Sub_1B90 (SPC audio command $19) and a write to dp:$60.

Phase 2 — VRAM index computation. A REP #$20 block loads the scroll bases from $1D0A/$1D0E into dp:$DB/$DD. Then N passes × 4 corner iterations call JSR Sub_1B36 to compute a tilemap word index (col×32 + row with $0400 wrap) for each of the four corners of a 2×2 tile block, offset by ADC $1D7C, and store the result into a $09CA–$09F8 VRAM slot.

Pass structure per corner block (62 bytes, invariant across all handlers): 

; Corner 1: (row, col) — X=col_idx, Y=row_idx already set
JSR Sub_1B36  →  CLC / ADC $1D7C  →  STA $09CA
; Corner 2: (row+1, col)
TYA / PHA / INC / AND #$003F / TAY / TXA / JSR Sub_1B36  →  CLC / ADC $1D7C  →  STA $09CC
; Corner 3: (row, col+1)  — restores pushed row
PLY / TXA / INC / AND #$001F / TAX / JSR Sub_1B36  →  CLC / ADC $1D7C  →  STA $09CE
; Corner 4: (row+1, col+1) — uses current Y/X from corner 3
TYA / INC / AND #$003F / TAY / TXA / JSR Sub_1B36  →  CLC / ADC $1D7C  →  STA $09D0

Row/col base selection per handler:

Handler Row bases Col bases Passes VRAM slots ModeE6_Handler $5B $5C, $5C−1 2 $09CA–$09D0, $09D2–$09D8 ModeEC_Handler $5B, $5B+1 $5C, $5C−1 4 $09CA–$09E8 ModeEE_Handler $5B−1, $5B $5C, $5C−1 4 $09CA–$09E8 ModeFA_Handler $5B, $5B+1 $5C, $5C−1, $5C−2 6 $09CA–$09F8 ModeFC_Handler $5B−1, $5B $5C, $5C−1, $5C−2 6 $09CA–$09F8

Pass 1 LDX anomaly. The compiler emits LDX $5B; TXA (3 bytes) instead of LDA $5B (2 bytes) for the row setup of every handler's first pass. All subsequent passes use LDA $5B normally. In Mode-EC and Mode-FA (positive row handlers), pass 1 has no additional modifier. In Mode-EE and Mode-FC (negative row handlers), pass 1 adds DEC A between TXA and ASL.

Tail. All handlers except ModeFC end with SEP #$20; LDA #$10; TSB $5F; BRL <raw_offset> to reach the default handler at $16DC. ModeFC sits immediately before $16DC and falls through without a BRL (tail is only SEP #$20; LDA #$10; TSB $5F).

dp:$60 value encodes the scroll update width: $00 = 2-entry (E6), $01 = 4-entry (EC/EE), $02 = 6-entry (FA/FC). This value is consumed by the default handler or the SPC audio subsystem.

docs.title: DefaultHandler ($C0:16DC–$18D8)
docs.text:
The DefaultHandler is the sixth arm of Sub_0C76's per-frame dispatch. It occupies 509 bytes immediately after ModeFC_Handler and is architecturally distinct from the five named mode handlers in several concrete ways.

Different layer-state variables. The named handlers (E6/EC/EE/FA/FC) read their layer-state index from dp:$5B/$5C. DefaultHandler reads from dp:$5D/$5E. This is not a convention difference — Sub_0C76 stores separate index values in each pair, and the handler uses whichever pair matches its role.

Different VRAM slots. The named handlers write their computed tilemap word-indices into the $09CA–$09F8 range. DefaultHandler writes to $09B2–$09B8 (four slots, one pass of 4 corners). The computation formula is identical (Sub_1B36 + ADC $1D7C), only the destination addresses differ.

Different SPC callee. The named handlers call Sub_1B90 with dp:$FC as the audio argument. DefaultHandler calls Sub_1BA7, a 4-byte wrapper that loads dp:$FB instead and then branches into Sub_1B90's body at the second instruction. The parameter register ($FB vs $FC) selects a different SPC command argument from the audio table.

No mode-table prologue. The named handlers begin by incrementing selected entries in the $7E:3000 layer-state table (2–6 entries depending on mode). DefaultHandler has no such prologue. Its VRAM section is conditional: it only runs if dp:$17 bit 1 is set, and only advances the layer-state entry if it reads $FE or $E0 (terminal values).

Bit-5 transition loop. After the optional VRAM section, DefaultHandler checks dp:$17 bit 5. If set, it clears it and enters a busy-loop: JSR $885A (a large unmatched frame-work routine) followed by JSR $00BF (VBlankHandler), repeating until dp:$38 reaches zero. After the loop it dispatches on dp:$45 (values 1–4) to one of four transition sub-modes, each calling a mode-specific renderer with DP temporarily set to $1D00, then tail-calling Sub_EC60.

Bit-0 scene-swap. If bit 5 was clear, DefaultHandler checks bit 0 of dp:$17. If set, it calls a scene-state probe at $024C. A carry-clear result triggers a full scene-swap sequence (JSL $C02C41, JSL $C10000, JSR $0B64/$0B75, etc.); carry-set takes a quick-clear path and tail-calls the $00EB fragment.

Summary of differences:

Attribute Named handlers (E6/EC/EE/FA/FC) DefaultHandler Layer-state index dp:$5B/$5C dp:$5D/$5E VRAM slots $09CA–$09F8 $09B2–$09B8 SPC callee Sub_1B90 (dp:$FC) Sub_1BA7 (dp:$FB) Mode-table prologue Yes (2–6 entries) No VRAM update Unconditional Conditional on dp:$17 bit 1 Post-VRAM action BRL tail to $16DC Bit-5/bit-0 section

docs.title: asar 1.91 Quirks
docs.text: Surprises encountered during this project. Future contributors: read this before spending an hour debugging a byte offset.

docs.title: 1. Named equate → STA generates LONG mode
docs.text:
Symptom: STA INIDISP emits opcode 8F (STA long, 4 bytes) instead of 8D (STA abs, 3 bytes). Every instruction downstream shifts by 1 byte.

Cause: When the operand is a named equate (e.g. INIDISP = $2100), asar promotes to 24-bit addressing regardless of the value's size.

Fix: Force abs mode with the .w suffix: 65C816 Assembly

STA.w INIDISP    ; $8D 00 21 — correct (3 bytes)
STA.w NMITIMEN   ; etc.
This applies to all hardware register writes where the register is defined as a named constant.

docs.title: 2. STX EquateName — "Unknown command"
docs.text:
Symptom: STX A1T7L (where A1T7L = $4372) produces an asar error.

Cause: asar 1.91 does not accept named equates as the operand for STX.

Fix: Use the raw hex literal: 65C816 Assembly

STX $4372        ; works fine

docs.title: 3. STA $0001,X → dp,X mode (not abs,X)
docs.text:
Symptom: STA $0001,X emits opcode 95 (dp,X) instead of 9D (abs,X). The value $0001 fits in 8 bits so asar defaults to direct-page indexed.

Fix: 65C816 Assembly

STA.w $0001,X    ; forces abs,X: $9D 01 00
Comes up in the PostVBlank OAM-fill loop.

docs.title: 4. BRL label stores the raw operand, not a target address
docs.text:
Symptom: BRL SomeLabel works fine. BRL $XXXX stores $XXXX as the branch offset directly, not the absolute address.

Cause: By design in asar. The BRL operand is a signed 16-bit offset from the next instruction, not an address. When you write BRL $XXXX, asar stores $XXXX literally.

Context in this project: VBlankHandler contains BRL $B193. That $B193 is the raw signed offset that lands at PostVBlank ($C0:B271) — it is NOT the address $B193.

Fix: When matching a BRL, extract the signed 16-bit operand from the ROM bytes and use it directly: 65C816 Assembly

BRL $B193        ; raw offset, not an address label
Using a label reference like BRL PostVBlank would likely produce a different offset.

docs.title: 5. JSR EquateName — "Unknown command"
docs.text:
Symptom: Similar to the STX issue — JSR SomeEquate fails.

Fix: Define a label stub at the target address with org: 65C816 Assembly

org $C0B309
Sub_B309:        ; no bytes emitted — just a label for JSR to resolve

; ... later, or elsewhere:
    JSR Sub_B309 ; resolves correctly to $B309

docs.title: 6. LDA #$7F in M=0 context: ROM uses 2-byte form, asar emits 3 bytes
docs.text:
Symptom: LDA #$7F in a 16-bit accumulator (M=0) context assembles as $A9 $7F $00 (3 bytes: immediate sign-zero-extended to 16 bits). If the ROM contains the 2-byte sequence $A9 $7F followed by an unrelated byte, make diff will show a 1-byte shift.

Cause: With M=0, LDA immediate is a 3-byte instruction. The assembler always emits the full 16-bit operand even if the value fits in 8 bits.

When it occurs: The ROM sometimes stores $A9 $7F (2 bytes) intending the next byte to be the following instruction, not the high byte of the immediate. This happens when the compiler originally ran in M=1 mode or used an 8-bit trick that asar doesn't replicate automatically.

Fix: Emit the raw bytes directly: 65C816 Assembly

db $A9,$7F        ; forces the 2-byte sequence in M=0 context
Do not write LDA #$7F when in 16-bit accumulator mode and the ROM has only 2 bytes here.

Discovered: session 26, during Sub_E12A Phase 1 matching (LDA #$7F / STA $D2).

docs.title: 7. SBC #$NNNN / ADC #$NNNN in M=0 context: wrong encoding
docs.text:
Symptom: SBC #$0040 (or ADC #$0040, etc.) in a 16-bit accumulator (M=0) context may assemble to the 2-byte M=1 form ($E9 $40) rather than the correct 3-byte M=0 form ($E9 $40 $00). This causes a 1-byte shift and a cascade of mismatches downstream.

Cause: asar 1.91 does not always track the M flag correctly across REP #$20 when choosing immediate operand width for SBC and ADC.

When it occurs: Any SBC #$xxxx or ADC #$xxxx in M=0 (16-bit A) context, especially when the upper byte of the immediate is $00 (i.e., the value fits in 8 bits, making the 2-byte vs 3-byte ambiguity matter).

Fix: Emit the raw bytes directly, same pattern as the LDA #$7F workaround: 65C816 Assembly

REP #$20                        ; M=0
; instead of: SBC #$0040        (may emit 2 bytes)
db $E9,$40,$00                  ; SBC #$0040 — explicit 3-byte M=0 encoding
; instead of: ADC #$000E        (may emit 2 bytes)
db $69,$0E,$00                  ; ADC #$000E — explicit 3-byte M=0 encoding

The opcode bytes are: $E9 = SBC immediate, $69 = ADC immediate; followed by the 16-bit little-endian operand.

Discovered: session 35 (BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits); applies to all 16-bit SBC/ADC immediates in M=0 context. Confirmed again in session 36 (BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame).

docs.title: Sprite-Slot Init System ($C0:CB0A–$E129, 5,664 bytes, 15 routines) — COMPLETE
docs.text:
Identified in session 28; cluster closed in session 31; dispatcher layer closed in session 32. The system has two layers:

Dispatcher layer (sessions 28–32): Sub_CB0A reads bits 0-1 of $1201,X (sprite type) and BRL-tails to the matching OAM-staging routine (Sub_CDC8 / Sub_D124 / Sub_DD28). These are OAM-only updates with no VRAM DMA.

VRAM-DMA cluster ($CB3A–$DD27, sessions 28–31): Each sprite-slot init routine follows a shared template: 1. Check $1780,X for type $03 (special fast path that skips the gate) or JSR Sub_CB3A (animation-frame gate). 2. Frame-type check: compare result byte with $0F01,X; if same type already loaded, CLC+RTS (no re-init needed). 3. JSR to appropriate slot allocator (Sub_E952 / Sub_E97A / Sub_E9AA) for 1/2/3 sprite slots. 4. Set up WRAM multiplier parameters (slot × $28 or $50 tiles), compute $D3 = frame-data pointer (from $4216 + $1380,X). 5. 8- or 16-tile DMA loop: for each entry at [$D3],Y, BIT #$4000: set → JSR Sub_E534, clear → JSR Sub_E687. 6. For multi-pass routines: INC $1B00,X; SEC RTS (caller re-invokes for next pass).

Sub_CEF5 is a three-way dispatch (dual-slot): type-3 → 32-tile full inline; pass-counter==0 → BRL Sub_D28A; pass-counter>0 → BRL Sub_D30D.

Sub_D4F7 is a four-way dispatch (triple-slot): type-3 → early RTS; dispatches on $1B00,X pass counter (0/1/2+) combined with $0D00,X type ($68/non-$68): - pass 0, non-$68 → inline body at Sub_D546 (two 8-tile loops, WRAM base and WRAM+$200); SEC - pass 0, $68 → Sub_D608 (one 16-tile loop, WRAM base); SEC - pass 1, non-$68 → Sub_D68B (two 8-tile loops, WRAM base+$0100 / base+$0300; LDX $6D reload; SEP #$30); SEC - pass 1, $68 → Sub_D738 (two 8-tile loops, WRAM base+$0200 / base+$0400; same structure; SEP #$30); SEC - pass 2+, non-$68 → Sub_D7E5 (single 16-tile loop; OAM staging 12 Y-entries + 8+4 X-positions; SEP #$10 before OAM); CLC - pass 2+, $68 → Sub_DA69 (two 8-tile loops + OAM staging 12 Y-entries + 4+8 X-positions; SEP #$10 before OAM); CLC

Callees Sub_CB3A, Sub_E952, Sub_E97A, Sub_E9AA, Sub_E534, Sub_E687 are all matched.

docs.title: Bank $01 / $C1 — Battle Engine (scouted session 33)
docs.text:
File offset: $010000–$01FFFF

Overview (scouted session 33 via dscotton reference): Bank $C1 is the battle engine master bank. 63,904 code bytes (97% code density), 1,632 incbin bytes, 481 named routines in the reference disassembly. The bank is one large coherent subsystem — nearly every byte is code, with no embedded large data tables. The only JSL from matched bank $C0 code into $C1 is the JSL $C10000 (Battle_Main) call from VBlankHandler.

Bank $C1 structure (high level): - $C10000–$C10018: Entry vector table (6 × JMP.W stubs); Battle_Main, BattleSys_ServiceEntry, and four named entry vectors - $C1001B–$C10044: Bootstrap sequence — JML to $CFFB65 (Battle_Bootstrap), JSL/JSR init chain - $C10045–$C10064: BattleSys_ServiceDispatch (10-service dispatcher via jump table) + incbin table data - $C10065–$C10088: BattleSys_Dispatch1006B (ASL/JSR dispatch) + four JML stubs + BattleSys_PumpFrames (frame wait loop) - $C10089–$C1010C: Math utility cluster — Battle_Mul8 (8×8 HW multiply), Battle_MulAccum (multiply-accumulate), Battle_Divide (16÷8 HW divide) - $C1010D–$C1011E: Shift helpers — Battle_ShiftLeft7/4/3, Battle_ShiftRight6/5/4/3 - $C1011F+: BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits, number formatting, BattleUI subsystem, BattleMenu, EnemyAI_SpatialService, battle animation, etc.

Session 34: Opened Bank $C1. Matched the math utility cluster ($C1:0089–$C1:011E, 150 bytes, 10 routines). Self-contained leaf routines with no dependencies on the larger battle WRAM layout.

Session 35: Matched number-display cluster ($C1:011F–$C1:01F8, 218 bytes, 3 routines) and trig/geometry cluster ($C1:01F9–$C1:0298, 160 bytes, 2 routines). Caller audit: Battle_Mul8 called from 11 sites, Battle_MulAccum from 13, Battle_Divide from 13. BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame (starts at $C1:0299) is the next target.

Session 36: Matched status-bar UI cluster ($C1:0299–$C1:05A6 + $C1:104E–$C1:106D, 814 bytes, 2 routines + 2 internal sub-labels). BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame (782 B) formats the full battle status bar: tilemap clear loop, three gauge-type layouts (HP+MaxHP+MP / HP+MP / HP+MP+TP), PC name panels, digit formatting via BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits, enemy name section. BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros (32 B) at $C1:104E suppresses leading-zero digits.

Session 37: Matched five callee routines of BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame ($C1:06F0–$C1:095C, 621 bytes). BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar (149 B) renders the ATB gauge bar via HW divide. BattleSys_SlotPanelRefresh (153 B) writes a 6-row×7-col panel strip using one of two tile tables. BattleMenu_DrawReadyWindowEdges (202 B) draws command-window border strips for all active PC slots and repaints the active-PC column (includes externally-callable sub-entry BattleUI_ClearActivePanelColumn at $0872). BattleUI_SetPanelAttrColumn (65 B) fills a 5-tile×2-col attribute column from $CCFA29/$CCFA23. BattleMenu_DrawWindowEdgeStrip (52 B) copies a 6-row border strip from $D159FC into the command-window tilemap. Note: the disassembler tool decoded several routines incorrectly (X-register size: should be 16-bit throughout); raw ROM bytes confirmed correct against reference.

Root-caused a disasm.py bug: the tool had been defaulting to X=1 (8-bit X/Y) for Bank $C1, causing all X-indexed addresses to decode one byte too short. Session 39: Matched the battle-menu item/tech list rendering cluster ($C1:095D–$C1:0C2C, 720 B, 8 routines). BattleMenu_RenderItemListRows clears a $0180-byte tilemap block and loops over 3 item rows via RenderItemRow. Three tail helpers (CODE_JP_C10BB6, BlankMpCostDigits, CODE_JP_C10C00) blank and copy formatted text into the two tilemap planes. One dead RTS byte at $0BB5 (unreachable after a JMP) reproduced exactly with db $60.

docs.title: Battle Menu Item/Tech List Rendering Cluster ($C1:095D–$C1:0C2C) — COMPLETE (session 39)
docs.text:
Battle-menu item and tech name list rendering for the battle command window. Entry state: M=1 (8-bit A), X=0 (16-bit X/Y), DP=0. Names are MVN'd from ROM bank $CC string tables into WRAM $7E:94A0, re-encoded by BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer, then copied with $2D attribute bytes into the two tilemap planes ($9A__ / $99__ base addresses, indexed by $82). Tilemap block clear uses X=16-bit to drive a DEX/BNE countdown over $0180 bytes.

Key WRAM: $7E:1580,X item ID, $7E:1582,X item flags, $7E:1583,X item count, $7E:94D0 tech ID array, $7E:1CDB tech availability flags, $7E:95D5 active-PC index, $7E:95EB,X active-PC tech base index, $7E:82/$83/$86/$87/$88 temp loop counters.

Quirks (session 39): One dead RTS byte at $C1:0BB5 (unreachable after JMP CODE_JP_C10C00) reproduced as db $60. No CLC before ADC #$0B5E in BattleMenu_RenderItemRow — the preceding SBC already sets carry correctly. All 16-bit ADC/SBC immediates encoded as db $69/$E9 raw bytes per asar quirk #4. STA.w $0000,Y requires .w suffix to force 3-byte absolute-indexed form rather than the 2-byte DP-indirect form.

docs.title: Battle Menu Window Upkeep Cluster ($C1:0C2D–$C1:104D + $C1:1C3A–$C1:1C49) — COMPLETE (session 40)
docs.text:
Per-frame window maintenance layer, called from the battle frame tick. BattleMenu_UpdateWindows is the top-level dispatcher called via entry vector at $C10012 (JMP BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL → eventually reaches here for submenu types 0/1). The cluster directly calls back into the already-matched status-bar cluster ($C10299, $C105A7, $C10872) — confirming those are a shared lower layer. BattleMenu_UpdateTechWindow (471 B) is the largest routine, handling the full tech-window refresh pass in one body that falls through into BattleMenu_DrawTechCursorRow.

Architecture: - UpdateWindows ($0C2D): dispatcher — JSL $CFFD9E (BattleFx_SetPtrA2FromTable), then switch on $95DB: 0=main, 1=tech, 2/other=idle - UpdateMainWindow ($0C49): ties back to status-bar cluster; handles PC-change detection ($A6DD vs $A6DF), panel refresh, JSL $CFFD02 (queue $0CC0 VRAM upload) - UpdateTechWindow ($0C83): full tech window refresh: copies text buffer, composes $CCFA95 border tiles (6 rows × 9 cols), fills MP digit cells per PC, resolves cursor slot via $CCF38C/$9551/$CCF3A1, copies battler struct fields $1A80–$1A86 to $9EE3–$9EE9 - DrawTechCursorRow ($0E5A): draws/clears $60–$63 cursor tiles; JSL $CD0027 (info panel text), JSL $CFFD36 (queue $A6E1 VRAM upload) - UpdateTechMpAvail ($0EE1): per-row affordability sweep — checks each PC's MP against $1A83/$1A85/$1A86 costs, slot-ready predicate, lock flag; writes $29/$2D attr to $A6E2/$A722 columns - LoadCommandWindowMap ($1C3A): isolated 16-byte leaf in the gap; copies $180 bytes from $D15800 (TechBoxBattles) into $0B40

Key asar pattern (session 40): CODE_JP_C1103D (shared exit RTS at $103D) is jumped to from three separate routines (UpdateMainWindow, DrawTechCursorRow, and is the fall-through tail of UpdateTechMpAvail). Must be a global label. Similarly, all internal loop labels in UpdateTechMpAvail use global CODE_JP_C10F28 / CODE_JP_C1100F / _L1001 / _ump_* style rather than local .labels to avoid asar's scope-reset-at-global-label issue (quirk #6).

docs.title: Menu Dirty-Flag Gate + Cursor Sprite ($C1:10E3–$C1:1152) — session 41
docs.text:
Two near-identical dirty-flag gates sit directly above the window-upkeep cluster, plus one adjacent small routine. BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL is the JSL-entry twin, reached from other banks via the cross-bank vector at $C10012 (JSL $C10012 → same-bank JMP $C110E3, no stack manipulation, so it returns via RTL to satisfy the original long call). BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyAndTick is a plain same-bank JSR target used by the battle-phase state machine, with an extra JSL $CD0009 per-frame service tick before its RTS. Both share an identical body: if WRAM $993A (menu-dirty flag) is set, clear it and run the rebuild chain BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler → BattleMenu_UpdateWindows → BattleMenu_ProcessInput → BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay. The latter three are not yet matched — added as org+bare-label stubs (same pattern as Bank $C0's forward references) so the JSRs resolve.

BattleMenu_DrawCursorSprites builds the 4-tile OAM entries for the command-window selection cursor at $0700, using a fixed template at ROM $CCF604–$CCF607 offset by per-slot coordinates $1D0C/$1D23; the attribute byte's palette bits come from $9F46 each call.

docs.title: Command-Window Input Handling ($C1:1153–$C1:127A + $C1:179C–$C1:17A0 + $C1:1B55–$C1:1B66) — session 41
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ProcessInput is the per-frame input dispatcher called from the dirty-flag gates. It reads two pad-edge bytes: $EE (button bits — bit $80 confirm, bit $40 a cursor-save-mode shortcut) and $EF (D-pad bits — $02 left, $08 up, $04 down, $01 right). Early exits: no active PC ($95D5 < 0) or target-select mode active ($9609 != 0, → BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput, stub). Submenu type $95DB routes to BattleMenu_TechListInput/BattleMenu_ItemListInput (both stubs) for types 1/2; type 0 (main menu) polls the pad-edge bytes and dispatches to the four small routines below, or to BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand (stub — the confirm-dispatch entry, itself branching into three large per-row command-execution paths, deliberately left for a future session).

BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev/CycleActivePcNext (Left/Right) decrement/increment the active-PC index $A6DD with wraparound, skipping slots whose $A6D9 entry is invalid, and carry the menu cursor row $95DC from the old slot to the new one. Both have a branch on $A0D4 (cursor-position-save setting) that copies from a $9916 per-PC default-row table instead — the reference disassembly marks this path unreachable in the shipped game, but it was reproduced byte-exact regardless (matching the ROM is the goal, not judging live reachability). BattleMenu_CursorUp/CursorDown (Up/Down) just move $95DC for the active slot and flag a redraw via $A43F.

Battle_ZeroResultEE (5 B, at $C1:179C — not contiguous with the rest of this cluster) and Battle_StopSfx (18 B, at $C1:1B55) are two small shared-tail leaves pulled in as callees. Battle_StopSfx reuses the exact $1E00–$1E02 + JSL $C70004 SPC-command pattern already seen in bank $C0's Sub_1B90 — same audio-command dispatch convention, different call site.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_ProcessInput $C1:1153–$C1:11E0 142 Matched Input dispatcher: pad-edge poll, submenu/cursor/confirm routing BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev $C1:11E1–$C1:1217 55 Matched Left: decrement $A6DD (wrap 0..2), skip invalid slots BattleMenu_CycleActivePcNext $C1:1218–$C1:124F 56 Matched Right: mirror of CycleActivePcPrev, wrap at 3 BattleMenu_CursorUp $C1:1250–$C1:1263 20 Matched Up: decrement $95DC, wrap 0..2, flag $A43F BattleMenu_CursorDown $C1:1264–$C1:127A 23 Matched Down: increment $95DC, wrap at 3, flag $A43F Battle_ZeroResultEE $C1:179C–$C1:17A0 5 Matched Shared tail: STZ $EE / STZ $EF / RTS Battle_StopSfx $C1:1B55–$C1:1B66 18 Matched SPC audio cmd $19 dispatcher (same pattern as C0's Sub_1B90)

docs.title: Confirm Dispatch ($C1:127B–$C1:131F) — session 41 (continued)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand is the entry point every confirm path in the input-handling cluster above eventually reaches. It sets a sentinel byte at $A0D7 (compared elsewhere — e.g. in BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame — to force a redraw), reloads the active-PC pointer, then reads the active PC's menu cursor row ($95DC,X: 0/1/2) and tail-jumps to one of three row handlers.

BattleMenu_ChooseAttack (row 0) is the simplest: it sets target mode $960D = $07, builds the valid-target list via BattleMenu_BuildTargetList ($C11F79, matched separately below), and enters target-select mode by incrementing $9609 — from here on, BattleMenu_ProcessInput's early-exit check routes input to BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput instead of the main menu. BattleMenu_OpenTechList/OpenItemList (rows 1/2) are less about targeting and more about UI state: each renders its list (reusing BattleMenu_RenderTechListRows/RenderItemListRows from session 39), flips the submenu type ($95DB), and — for items — copies a $180-byte window graphic (ItemBoxBattles, ROM $D15BD0) into the command-window tilemap. Both are gated on $A0A7, apparently a "list locked" flag of some kind.

This closes the confirm dispatcher itself, but not what's behind it: BattleMenu_TechListInput/ItemListInput/TargetSelectInput (the actual list-navigation and confirm-within-a-list logic) remain stubs.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand $C1:127B–$C1:129B 33 Matched Sets sentinel $A0D7, tail-jumps on cursor row to row handler BattleMenu_ChooseAttack $C1:129C–$C1:12BB 32 Matched Row 0: target mode $960D=$07, BuildTargetList, enter target-select BattleMenu_OpenTechList $C1:12BC–$C1:12EC 49 Matched Row 1: render tech list + avail flags, $95DB=1, mark $A86A BattleMenu_OpenItemList $C1:12ED–$C1:131F 51 Matched Row 2: render item list, copy ItemBoxBattles gfx, $95DB=2

docs.title: Target-List Initializer ($C1:1F79–$C1:1FDC) — session 41 (continued once more)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_BuildTargetList is called by BattleMenu_ChooseAttack above, and — per the reference disassembly — also from the still-unmatched tech-confirm and item-confirm paths deeper in TechListInput/ItemListInput. It resets target-selection state ($9613, $960A, $960C, $A64F, $A6D8), blanks two 11-entry lists ($99C0-$99CA candidates, $A62D-$A637 selections) to $FF, and — unless a target-select-to-cancel state is already active — snapshots the current submenu type into $A86B so cancelling target-select returns to the right screen.

The actual per-mode target collection is fully deferred: the routine clamps $960D (target mode) into $00-$20, doubles it into a word index, and does an indexed-indirect JSR ($1FF8,X) into a jump table this session left completely unmatched. That table and its handlers (BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets at $C12045 — the shared tail most handlers fall into, scanning candidate slots and compacting the list — BattleTgt_ListEnemiesSingle at $C120A9, and several more visible in the reference disassembly) are a large, self-contained targeting subsystem: the same "reference a dispatch table by raw address, match the table's contents later" pattern already used for bank $C0's $5D6E entity-dispatch table.

One real bug surfaced while matching this: an early draft nested the list-clearing LDA #$FF inside the clear-loop instead of before it. Functionally harmless (A is reloaded with the same constant each iteration either way) but it shifts the loop's start address, which changes the BPL branch's relative offset by one byte — make diff caught it immediately as a single-byte mismatch at $C1:1F9C. A reminder that a "looks equivalent" restructuring of a loop body can still produce different bytes even when the logic is unchanged.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_BuildTargetList $C1:1F79–$C1:1FDC 100 Matched Reset target state, blank candidate/selection lists, dispatch via unmatched $1FF8 table

docs.title: Ready-Battler Dequeue ($C1:1B67–$C1:1BA9) — session 41 (final increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler closes out the last stub callee referenced by the menu dirty-flag gates matched at the start of today's session. It pops the head of a small FIFO — WRAM $95D6-$95D9, three deep, live count in $95DA — that holds battler slots whose ATB gauge has filled and are now ready to act. Dequeuing restores that battler's saved menu-cursor position ($A863/$A866 → $95DF/$95EB, the same save/restore pair BattleMenu_TechListCancel uses), marks the slot present in the roster by writing its own index into $A6D9,X (an identity-map — this project has seen $A6D9,X used as a presence/validity check via BMI elsewhere, e.g. BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev), forces a command-window reload sentinel, shifts the queue down one slot, and — if no PC was already active — promotes the newly-dequeued battler to active.

Immediately adjacent at $C11BAA sits BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady (service 2 of the $C10045 cross-bank service-dispatch API first documented back when Bank $C1 was opened) — the inverse operation, thematically, and matched right after in the same session (see below).

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler $C1:1B67–$C1:1BA9 67 Matched Pop ATB-ready queue head, restore cursor pos, mark roster slot present, shift queue, claim active-PC if none set

docs.title: Ready-Battler Remove ($C1:1BAA–$C1:1C39) — session 41 (final increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady is service 2 of the $C10045 cross-bank service-dispatch API, and the structural inverse of DequeueReadyBattler just above it: instead of pulling a battler into the active state, it takes one out, whether that battler is currently sitting in the 3-deep ready queue or is the actively-displayed menu PC.

The queued case reuses a familiar shape — scan the queue for a match, then shift everything after it down by one — generalized from DequeueReadyBattler's always-shift-from-zero version to start from wherever the match was found. The active-PC case is meatier: if the battler being removed isn't the one currently on screen, it's a quiet removal (clear its roster slot, force a redraw). If it is the displayed PC, the routine also cancels any open submenu or target-selection state, then walks the roster looking for another valid slot to promote to active — or, if none exist, explicitly marks "no active PC."

This routine reproduced the exact same class of bug as BattleMenu_BuildTargetList earlier in the session: an early draft put a one-time LDA $80 inside the queue-scan loop instead of before it, which shifts where the loop's branch target sits and changes the branch's offset byte. Two occurrences of an identical mistake in one sitting is a pattern, not a coincidence — worth remembering that a single-byte make diff mismatch landing on what looks like a branch instruction, near a loop, is a strong signal to check whether a setup instruction got nested one line too deep.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady $C1:1BAA–$C1:1C39 144 Matched Remove queued/active battler from ready state; cancel submenu/targeting + promote next active if it was displayed

docs.title: Target-Select Input ($C1:1561–$C1:1619) — session 41 (seventh increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput is the per-frame input handler active whenever $9609 (target-select mode) is nonzero — reached from BattleMenu_ProcessInput's very first branch, and entered by BattleMenu_ChooseAttack back in the confirm-dispatch cluster. Every call rebuilds the target list from scratch via BattleMenu_BuildTargetList, then either cancels (no valid target found, or the cancel button) or polls for confirm/cycle-target input.

The cancel path is the meatier half: it restores whichever submenu was open before targeting started ($A86B), and — depending on whether that was the tech list or item list — either just re-flags the tech window active or fully reloads the $180-byte item-window graphic (ItemBoxBattles, the same ROM data BattleMenu_OpenItemList uses). Both paths converge on a shared cursor-highlight update: OR the OAM high-table byte with $55 and set four cursor-sprite X-positions to $F0.

The confirm/cycle path is comparatively simple — check $EE bits $C0 for confirm (tail-jump to BattleMenu_CommitAction, matched separately below), or $EF bits for cycling the target selection forward/backward (BattleMenu_TargetNext/TargetPrev, also matched below) — unless $960C's target-all flag is set, in which case cycling is disabled entirely.

A genuinely dead 18-byte block. Between the tech-return and confirm/cycle sections sits a near-exact duplicate of the item-graphic copy loop: same TDC/TAX/copy/INX/CPX #$0180 shape, but its loop-continue BNE targets the confirm/cycle section's entry point instead of looping back on itself. The practical effect is that if this block ever executed, it would run exactly one iteration before falling out of the "loop" into unrelated code — it's not a working copy at all. More importantly, nothing in the routine's actual control flow reaches it: every path that could have fallen into it branches past it with an unconditional BRA instead. This is the first genuinely dead block (as opposed to a single stray byte, like session 39's dead RTS) found in Bank $C1. Reproduced byte-for-byte as unreachable code, per the project's standing policy of matching the ROM exactly rather than only the parts that still do something.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput $C1:1561–$C1:1619 185 Matched Per-frame target-select input; rebuild target list, cancel-to-prior-submenu or poll confirm/cycle-target; 18 dead bytes reproduced

docs.title: Command-Commit Cluster ($C1:161A–$C1:179B) — session 41 (eighth and final increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_CommitAction is the routine every confirm path in the entire command-menu neighborhood ultimately reaches — attack today, and tech/item once those submenus are matched (BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput's confirm branch tail-jumps straight here). It's the largest single routine matched in this whole cluster (308 B), and it's where a player's menu selections finally turn into a concrete battle command.

The shape is a three-way dispatch on $95DB (attack/tech/item) that fills in type-specific fields, followed by a shared tail that all three converge on. Attack is trivial — just a type flag and "no id" sentinel. Tech is the most involved: it optionally saves the menu cursor position, then — critically — "consumes" the partner battler(s) for dual- and triple-techs via BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot, once for the primary partner (low nibble of $9EE7) and again for a second partner if the high nibble indicates a triple-tech. Item decrements the item's stock count and clears the item-list scroll position.

The shared tail builds an 8-byte command record at $93EE plus an offset resolved through the same $CCFAF0 slot-to-sprite-index lookup table ConsumePartnerSlot also uses — type byte, a flag byte, submenu type, target, and the tech/item id pair — increments the queued-command count, then clears the confirming PC's roster slot and searches for another valid slot to promote to active, reusing the exact same scan-and-fallback shape BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady used earlier today.

BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot itself is a tight 30-byte leaf: mark the given slot's roster presence gone, decrement the active-PC count if it was currently active, and clear the "queued" bit of its sprite flag byte. BattleMenu_TargetNext/TargetPrev are D-pad cycling helpers for the target cursor ($9614), structurally identical to BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev/Next from earlier in the session — advance/decrement with wraparound, skip invalid candidate-list entries. TargetPrev doesn't even need its own RTS; it falls straight through into the already-matched Battle_ZeroResultEE since the two are adjacent in ROM.

This closes the entire span from $C1:161A to $C1:179B, connecting directly into Battle_ZeroResultEE — meaning the whole neighborhood from the menu dirty-flag gate ($C1:10E3) through target confirmation is now one continuous matched region, apart from the two remaining submenu-input stubs (TechListInput, ItemListInput, the former closed in the next session — see below) and BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_CommitAction $C1:161A–$C1:1749 308 Matched Build command record for confirmed action; type dispatch, partner consumption, enqueue, advance active-PC BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot $C1:174E–$C1:176B 30 Matched Remove dual/triple-tech partner from ready state BattleMenu_TargetNext $C1:176C–$C1:1785 26 Matched Advance target cursor, skip invalid entries BattleMenu_TargetPrev $C1:1786–$C1:179B 22 Matched Decrement target cursor, skip invalid entries; falls through to Battle_ZeroResultEE

docs.title: Tech-List Input Cluster ($C1:1320–$C1:143C) — session 41 (ninth increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TechListInput is the per-frame dispatcher for the tech submenu, computing the highlighted tech's list index (scroll position plus cursor row) before polling pad-edge bytes for confirm, cancel, and up/down. BattleMenu_TechConfirm hands off to targeting the same way BattleMenu_ChooseAttack does — set a target mode, build the target list, enter target-select mode if a valid target exists. BattleMenu_TechListCancel is the smallest of the five: restore the saved cursor/scroll pair and return to the main menu.

BattleMenu_TechListPrev and TechListNext are the pair worth slowing down for. Moving the tech cursor isn't a plain increment or decrement, because some techs in the list are unavailable (insufficient MP, not yet learned, etc. — tracked via a per-slot availability byte at $1CDB) and have to be skipped over rather than landed on. Both routines walk one step at a time from the current list index looking for the next available entry, counting how many steps that took — then replay that same step count against the separate (cursor row, scroll offset) pair that actually controls what's drawn on screen, scrolling the visible window by one row at a time whenever the cursor would go outside the visible 0–2 range. It's a two-coordinate-systems problem (list index vs. screen position) solved by counting the distance in one and walking it in the other, and it's structurally identical between the "up" and "down" directions apart from which way the walk goes and which end of the list bounds it.

This closes the tech submenu entirely — BattleMenu_ItemListInput (matched immediately after, see below) was the only remaining submenu-input stub.

Block SNES addr Bytes Status Description BattleMenu_TechListInput $C1:1320–$C1:1368 73 Matched Per-frame tech-list input dispatcher BattleMenu_TechConfirm $C1:1369–$C1:138E 38 Matched Confirm highlighted tech, hand off to targeting BattleMenu_TechListCancel $C1:138F–$C1:13AC 30 Matched Close tech list, restore saved cursor/scroll BattleMenu_TechListPrev $C1:13AD–$C1:13F3 71 Matched Walk to previous available tech, resync cursor/scroll, scroll up if needed BattleMenu_TechListNext $C1:13F4–$C1:143C 73 Matched Mirror of TechListPrev, bounded by list length, scroll down if needed

docs.title: Item-List Input Cluster ($C1:143D–$C1:1560 + $C1:17A1–$C1:17DC) — session 41 (tenth and final increment)
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ItemListInput mirrors TechListInput's dispatcher shape (confirm/cancel/up/down via the same pad-edge bit tests) with two extra branches: $EE bits $20/$10 let the player page the whole list up or down 3 rows at once, and a check of $A0D0 triggers a full re-render when some other part of the engine has flagged the display stale. BattleMenu_ItemConfirm is structurally close to BattleMenu_TechConfirm — resolve a record index, reject if unusable, then hand off to targeting — but item records are a flat array ($1580, 5-byte stride: id/target-mode/flags/quantity + one padding byte) rather than the tech system's bitmask-based availability check.

The interesting architectural difference from the tech list shows up in cursor movement. Techs need step-counting-and-skip logic because some entries are unselectable; items don't have that problem (unusable items are presumably still just... items — the render routine handles greying them out, but the cursor still lands on them). So BattleMenu_ItemCursorUp/CursorDown are almost trivial: move the row, and only call out to a scroll helper (ItemListScrollUp/ScrollDown) when the cursor is already at the top or bottom of the visible window.

A sub-entry-point pattern, reused from bank $C0. BattleMenu_ItemListPageDown/PageUp don't call the render routine directly — they set the scroll position themselves, then JSR into the middle of ItemListScrollDown/ScrollUp, landing exactly on the internal JSR BattleMenu_RenderItemListRows instruction and reusing everything after it (the render call plus the scroll-arrow indicator writes) as a shared tail. This is the same "call into another routine's tail as a mini-subroutine" trick already seen in bank $C0's Sub_1BA7 (an alternate entry into Sub_1B90). Because the entry point is referenced from a different routine's scope, it has to be a real global label rather than a local .dot label — a direct application of the asar local-scope-reset quirk this project has documented before.

A genuinely redundant branch. BattleMenu_ItemListScrollUp opens with two consecutive BEQ instructions testing the exact same (unmodified) zero flag. The first one's target is reachable; the second one's isn't — by the time execution reaches the second check, the first check has already proven the flag clear, so the second BEQ can never fire. It's not dead code (the bytes execute every single call), just a dead branch — a distinction from the fully-unreachable block found in BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput earlier this session. Reproduced exactly either way.

A correction to session 39. Working out BattleMenu_ItemConfirm's exact field layout ($1580=id, $1583=quantity) revealed that BattleMenu_RenderItemRow's inline comments — written back in session 39, before this part of the item system was understood — had those two swapped (labeling $1583,X "item ID" and $1580,X "unconfirmed-animation / display flag"). Fixed both comments; no byte changes, since comments don't affect matching.

This closes the item submenu, and with it, every submenu-input handler in the entire command-menu subsystem. BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay is now the only remaining single-routine stub in this whole neighborhood.

docs.title: Cursor Overlay ($C1:17DD–$C1:1B18) — session 42
docs.text:
BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay runs once per frame at the end of the menu rebuild chain and draws whatever cursor belongs on screen. It is effectively four routines behind one dispatcher: no active PC → hide the 4 main-cursor OAM slots ($0700–$070F, visibility bits in $0900); tech list → the normal single cursor, or for a dual/triple tech (tech id ≥ $39) one sprite over the caster and one over each partner, partners decoded from the nibble pair in $9EE7 ($F = none); item list → change-tracked redraws of the scroll arrows ($0EFC/$0FFC, cached in $9920) and the 4-tile row highlight ($CCFAE9 pointer table, cached in $991F), queuing JSL $CFFD6A only if either changed; target select → a single cursor (with an enemy info-panel dispatch through JSL $CD0030/$CD002D in the main Attack menu, gated by the per-enemy table $E1DE80) or a multi-target sweep.

The multi-target sweep is the notable piece: with only four cursor sprites, it draws three selection-list entries per frame, saves its position in $960B, and resumes there next frame, wrapping after six — so the cursors alternate between target groups across frames rather than all being drawn at once.

Every cursor placement uses the same inlined idiom: $1D0C,X/$1D23,X (base origin, shared with DrawCursorSprites) + $9708,X/$9713,X (per-battler live offset, X = any of the 11 battler slots) − $10.

With this matched, the span $C1:1320–$C1:1B18 is continuous and the command-menu subsystem has no stubs left.

docs.title: Target-Mode Layer ($C1:1B19–$C1:1B54 + $C1:1FDD–$C1:2331 + $C1:27C5–$C1:283C) — session 43
docs.text:
BattleMenu_EnqueueReadyBattler (service 1 of the $C10045 API) is the entry side of the ATB-ready queue that DequeueReadyBattler drains: it skips battlers already in the roster, sets bit 7 ("waiting for command") of the battler's $93EE flag byte, appends to $95D6+count, resets the cursor row to $9916,X, and plays SPC command $19 with sound $42.

BattleTgt_ModeTable (33 words at $1FF8) maps target mode $960D&$7F to 18 handlers. List modes (single/all ally, single/all enemy, everyone) are presets of a slot range and the target-all flag, entering the shared builder BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets. Bespoke modes: Self, SingleKoAlly (PC status bit 7), and PcByCharId4/5 (find a party member by $2980,X id). Area modes anchor on the caster, an aimed enemy, or party member id 3/6, fill $9604–$9608 ($9605 source, $9606 aim, $9607 shape/size, $9608 variant), call one of four geometry routines, and select every resulting candidate. BattleTgt_RunAreaQuery (service 7) exposes those same geometry routines outside the bank.

docs.title: How to update this file
docs.text:
1. Run python3 tools/disasm.py roms/chrono_trigger.sfc <bank_hex> to sweep a bank
  2. Add known code/data regions to the table above
  3. As functions get matched, change their status from Unmapped → Matched
  4. Run python3 tools/progress.py --update to regenerate PROGRESS.md stats

docs.title: CI Setup
docs.text: The GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/match.yml runs make diff on every PR and push to main, verifying byte-exact reassembly.

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text: Because the ROM cannot be committed to the repo, CI needs it supplied as a GitHub Actions secret encoded in base64.

docs.title: 1. Encode your ROM
docs.text:
Shell
base64 -w 0 roms/chrono_trigger.sfc > /tmp/rom_b64.txt

docs.title: 2. Add it as a repository secret
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
  2. Click New repository secret
  3. Name: ROM_B64
  4. Value: paste the content of /tmp/rom_b64.txt

The workflow restores the ROM, verifies its SHA256 against docs/ROM_HASH.md, builds with make, and runs diff_rom.py. If the hash doesn't match or the diff fails, the job errors.

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text: Open a PR that touches any .asm file — the check should appear automatically.

docs.title: If you don't have the secret set
docs.text: The workflow degrades gracefully: it emits a warning and skips the byte-exact check. This means the CI still runs (environment check, etc.) but won't fail on an unmatched ROM. Contributors without repo secrets can still run locally via make diff.

docs.title: Local workflow (no CI needed)
docs.text:
Shell
python3 tools/check_env.py   # confirm asar + python3 present
make diff                    # build and compare
python3 tools/progress.py    # show current byte coverage stats

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This project is early enough that the most valuable contributions right now are structural, not just function-matching:

docs.title: Ways to help
docs.text:
• Bank mapping — identifying what lives where in ROM, even roughly, before anything is matched
  • Function matching — the core loop: disassemble → label → verify byte-exact reassembly (see README "Workflow")
  • Tooling — better diffing, automated progress tracking, CI
  • Data/graphics cataloging — identifying compressed blobs, tile data, and their formats (separate from code matching, but needed eventually)

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
• No ROM data, headers, or extracted assets in commits. Ever. Tools and source only. If in doubt, don't commit it.
  • Byte-exact means byte-exact. A function that "looks equivalent" but doesn't reassemble identically isn't matched yet — logically-equivalent but differently-encoded assembly is common on 65816 and needs to be resolved before marking something done.
  • Cite your reasoning in labels/comments. When you name a routine or variable, leave a short comment on how you inferred its purpose (trace output, cross-reference, etc.) so others can verify or correct it.
  • One PR per logical unit — a bank section, a routine, a tooling change. Keeps review sane.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. python3 tools/check_env.py to confirm your toolchain
  2. Check docs/PROGRESS.md for open areas
  3. Drop your own legally-dumped ROM in roms/ (never committed)
  4. make diff should report a 100% match against a completely empty asm/main.asm — that's the correct starting state before you've matched anything
