docs.title: Next
docs.text: The default mode handler at $C0:16DC (~747 bytes), which needs Sub_1BA7 at $C0:1BA7 identified first. Then $C0:881E (frame DMA/controller update, ~60-byte body with a large callee tree). The $0C76 cluster will take more sessions: bottom-up through the handlers, then the $881E tree, then $18D9.

docs.title: 7 August 2026: the last mode handler, screen transitions, and the sprite init pass
docs.text: The $0C76 mode dispatch is closed with the default handler. Then the whole screen-transition path, from fade-out through scene save and restore to fade-in, is matched, two early labels are corrected, and the 1,034-byte sprite init pass Sub_E12A goes in: 2,568 new bytes in 15 functions over sessions 21 to 25.

docs.title: DefaultHandler closes the mode dispatch
docs.text:
DefaultHandler at $C0:16DC–$18D8 (509 bytes) is the last arm of Sub_0C76's per-frame dispatch. I already knew it used dp $5D/$5E instead of $5B/$5C and wrote VRAM slots $09B2–$09B8 instead of $09CA–$09F8. Almost nothing else matches the named handlers either. Those follow a tight template (advance some $7E:3000 entries, run N passes of 4-corner writes via Sub_1B36, BRL back to $16DC). DefaultHandler is $16DC, the landing zone, so there is no tail call.

Three bit flags in dp $17 control three separate sections:

  • Bit 1 (VRAM update). Clears the flag, calls Sub_1BA7, reads the layer entry at $7E:3000,X (index dp $5D) and advances it only for the terminal mode bytes $FE or $E0. Then one 4-corner VRAM pass to $09B2/$09B4/$09B6/$09B8, and bit 1 of dp $5F set as a done flag. The 16-bit math is the same as in the named handlers, with other sources and destinations.
  • Bit 5 (display-mode transition). The surprise. Clears the bit, sets dp $38 = 1, and loops: JSR $885A / JSR $00BF / check dp $38. After the loop (dp $38 = 0) it reads dp $45 and dispatches to one of four transition sub-modes (values 1–4). Each calls a mode-specific renderer with DP set to $1D00 for the call, adjusts dp $46, clears dp $45 and tail-calls Sub_EC60. Mode 3 runs three renderer passes with PHD/PLD framing and swaps dp $7C/$82 between them. No named handler has anything like this.
  • Bit 0 (scene swap). Checked only when bit 5 is clear. Calls a probe at $024C. Carry clear starts a full scene swap: JSL $C02C41, JSL $C10000 (bank $C1 init), reinstall NMI/IRQ, reset dp $17/$18, call three post-init helpers. Carry set takes a quick path: flip bits in $17/$18 and BRL to the $00EB fragment (JSR $881E + JSR $00DE + BRL $EC60).

Sub_1BA7 ($C0:1BA7–$1BAA, 4 bytes) sends an SPC audio command:

65C816 Assembly
LDA $FB        ; load dp:$FB as audio arg 0
BRA Sub_1B90_body  ; join Sub_1B90 at STA $1E01

Sub_1B90 uses dp $FC for the same argument. Sub_1BA7 loads $FB instead and jumps into Sub_1B90 at its second instruction, skipping only LDA $FC. A new Sub_1B90_body label marks that spot; labels emit no bytes, so Sub_1B90 is unchanged. $FB versus $FC presumably picks a different command from the SPC tables, which fits a different kind of layer transition.

$885A, deferred. The bit-5 loop calls it every frame until dp $38 clears. The disassembler traced over 2,700 unique instructions from it before hitting the sweep limit, into a large tree across bank $C0 ($7612, $77E4, $79CF, $7BA9 and many more). It is a major frame-work routine and is in the bank map as Identified/deferred. Sub_EC60 stays the always-deferred post-VBlank worker. DefaultHandler tail-calls it for sub-modes 1, 2 and 3 (raw BRL offsets $D49B, $D472 and $D3FE), and mode 4 reaches it with two JSRs.

Handler Status ModeE6_Handler Matched ModeEC_Handler Matched ModeEE_Handler Matched ModeFA_Handler Matched ModeFC_Handler Matched DefaultHandler Matched Sub_1B36 (leaf callee) Matched Sub_1B90 (leaf callee) Matched Sub_1BA7 (leaf callee) Matched Sub_EC60 (black-box) Identified, always-deferred Sub_885A (black-box) Identified, deferred

The mode-dispatch part of the $0C76 cluster is complete. Two subsystems are now fully closed: the sprite renderer cluster (fourteen functions, sessions 7–17) and the $0C76 mode dispatch (thirteen functions, sessions 18–21).

docs.title: The screen-transition manager
docs.text:
Past DefaultHandler's last byte ($18D8) sit routines that are not part of the Sub_0C76 tree.

Sub_18D9 ($C0:18D9–$1984, 172 bytes) is the outer gate for screen fades and mode transitions, called from the startup sequence at $C0:00A1. It reads two flags:

  • $00F0 bit 0: whether the game is in BG mode 5 (the high-resolution mode Chrono Trigger uses for map transitions)
  • $00F6 bits 0, 6 and 7: a second mode-control byte

If $00F0 bit 0 is set, it busy-waits: it steps the fade counter dp $19 down once per VBlank, calling JSL $FDC2C1 (the cross-bank fade update in bank $FD) and JSR $EC60 each time, until the bit clears. A "busy" flag at $0407 is written $FF at the top of every pass and reset to zero on exit. Then: if $00F6 bit 0 is set it calls Sub_1985. If $00F6 bit 6 is clear, it calls Sub_1ADF when dp $62 is non-zero. If bit 6 is set, it takes a long reinit path: the fade-down loop again, then $0B4E, $011B, JSL $C28000, $0B4E, $0B64, $0B75, DP=$0100, $01A5, $1A03, $B192, Sub_2824, and $0407 cleared. That is a full screen transition in this engine: fade out, tear down hardware state, reinit everything, run the post-transition fade.

Sub_1985 ($C0:1985–$19C6, 66 bytes) is the narrower mode-5 probe, called from Sub_18D9 at $191D. It checks:

  1. dp $26: if non-zero, XOR with $03, store and return (this flips between two palette modes)
  2. $7F0000: if below $49, bail
  3. dp $1F, dp $62, dp $10 in turn: any non-zero returns

If every guard passes, it runs the same fade-to-black loop (dp $19 down, JSL $FDC2C1, JSR $EC60), then calls $0B4E and $011B. There is no RTS. It falls straight into Sub_19C7, the mode-5 hardware reinit, so calling Sub_1985 when a reinit is needed runs Sub_19C7 on the way out. The first estimate said 322 bytes because tracing without knowing Sub_19C7 was already matched counts 66 + 60 bytes of Sub_19C7 and more. Seeing org $C019C7 / Sub_19C7: in the source made the boundary obvious.

Sub_1ADF ($C0:1ADF–$1B35, 87 bytes) is a pure leaf that runs an on-screen menu cursor, depending on dp $62:

  • $62 = 1: if dp $63 is not negative and not $04, copy it to dp $66 and set dp $63 = $04. Then, if $00F6 bit 7 is set, zero dp $34 (a word write).
  • $62 = 2: read joypad $00F7. Bit 2 (up) increments dp $63, clamped at dp $65; bit 3 (down) decrements it, floored at dp $64; bit 7 of $00F8 (Start) sets dp $62 = $03 and returns. Both clamps use BCS.
  • anything else: the same "check $63, update $66, set $63=$04" block as $62 = 1.

The fade-loop label bug. The first make diff had two wrong bytes, at 0x001957 and 0x0019C0: the BRA offsets in the fade loops of Sub_18D9 and Sub_1985, $EB (−21) instead of $E6 (−26). I had put .fade_loop after LDA #$FF / STA $0407, but the ROM re-runs those two instructions every pass. Moving the label back five bytes fixed both.

docs.title: Two names that were backwards
docs.text:
Cross-checking against dscotton's disassembly turned up two early labels that were wrong.

EntryTable → ReentryVectors. The table at $C0:0000 was commented as "boot modes". Entry 0, BRA GameLoop_Main, is right. But entries 1–4 are three-byte BRL stubs to ScrollStepAccum, AudioDrvSync, MusicCueDispatch and AudioFadeDispatch. These are JSL re-entry points. A caller in another bank does JSL $C0:0002 (or $0005, $0008, $000B), which pushes three bytes. The BRL jumps to the real target without pushing anything, and the target's RTL returns straight to the caller. The stubs give other banks fixed entry points. Callers turn up in bank $CD ($CD:043E, $CD:0C8C) and bank $D1 ($D1:F405, $D1:F4E2), and every target ends in RTL ($6B).

FrameUpdate → LoadLocation. The routine at $C0:00F4 was commented "per-frame logic dispatch", because GameLoop_Main calls it. But GameLoop_Main is the outer loop that runs once per mode entry; the per-frame loop is GameLoop_FrameBody at $C0:0097. The routine's ten JSRs and two JSLs load a location.

Both renames reached every call site and label stub. No bytes changed (ReentryVectors $C0:0000–$000D, 14 bytes; LoadLocation $C0:00F4–$011A, 39 bytes), and make diff was clean.

docs.title: Saving and restoring the scene
docs.text:
Sub_18D9's reinit path left four callees. Estimates were Sub_011B ~138 bytes (calls $0918, also called from Sub_0C76), Sub_01A5 unknown (calls $0905, also called from Sub_0C76), Sub_1A03 ~160 bytes (calls $597D), Sub_B192 ~32 bytes (BRL to $E935). All four are matched, plus three smaller callees:

  • Sub_011B ($C0:011B–$01A4, 138 bytes) saves the scene context to $7F:1Dxx. It skips the save if dp $29 is zero. It calls Sub_0918 to copy a 20,736-byte ($14E0) WRAM block from $00:0920 to $7F:2000 with MVN, then copies scene table pointers and scroll positions to $7F:1D09–$1D24.
  • Sub_01A5 ($C0:01A5–$024B, 167 bytes) is the full location-engine init. It calls Sub_0905 (the reverse copy), runs an audio tick (SEP #$10 / JSL $FDC2C1 / REP #$10 / JSL $FDC1EE), sets OAM base pointers ($7D=$0900, $7F=$0770, $7B=$08A0), calls eight scene-setup helpers, restores the scroll registers, calls Sub_595C, and calls $E12A depending on a flag.
  • Sub_0905 and Sub_0918 ($C0:0905–$0917 and $C0:0918–$092A, 19 bytes each) are the MVN pair. In the opcode bytes the destination bank comes first: Sub_0918 (save) is $54 $7F $00, from $00 to $7F; Sub_0905 (restore) is $54 $00 $7F. The disassembler also got the LDX/LDY sizes wrong here, assuming 8-bit X; the entry state is 16-bit X, so LDX #$2000 is three bytes.
  • Sub_1A03 ($C0:1A03–$1AAB, 169 bytes) restores the scene after a transition. It compares the current palette colors ($7E:2980–$2982) with the cached dp $94–$96; if they match, it returns early. Otherwise it calls Sub_597D for each of seven active sprite slots, updates the cache, copies scene table pointers back from $7F:1D09/$0F/$15, and restores dp $AB/$AC/$AD from $7F:1D1B/$1C/$1D. The addresses match Sub_011B's exactly: the pair is closed.
  • Sub_B192 ($C0:B192–$B1AF, 30 bytes) zeroes the $1Bxx table. It sets DP to $1B00, loads a loop count from $7F:2000, zeroes 16-bit words at $00,Y (Y steps by 2, count down to zero), restores DP and tail-calls Sub_E935 with BRL. The operand is the raw offset $3783, applied from the address after the BRL. I couldn't make the hand arithmetic land on $E935, but make diff passes with that raw offset.
  • Sub_E935 ($C0:E935–$E951, 29 bytes) sets DP to $0B00 and stores $80 into dp $C0–$C7, which is WRAM $0BC0–$0BC7. $80 means "no sprite" in the sprite system. This links back to Sub_E9E2/Sub_E9FF/Sub_EA1F, which search $0BC0 and mark slots with $80.

The full transition, now byte-exact end to end:

Text Only
fade out (VBlank loop decrementing dp:$19)
  → InitHW     (SEI + forced blank)
  → Sub_011B   (save scene context: MVN + scroll positions → $7F:1Dxx)
  → JSL $C28000 (set BG mode)
  → InitHW + InstallNMI + InstallIRQ
  → Sub_01A5   (full location init: MVN restore + 8 scene helpers + scroll restore)
  → Sub_1A03   (restore sprite colors + scene tables from $7F:1Dxx)
  → Sub_B192   (clear $1Bxx table → Sub_E935 → mark $0BC0–$0BC7 = $80)
  → Sub_2824   (post-transition fade loop)

The MVN idiom. The only MVN instructions in matched code are in Sub_0905 (54 00 7F: $7F:2000 → $00:0920) and Sub_0918 (54 7F 00: $00:0920 → $7F:2000), called from Sub_01A5 and Sub_011B. The address pair appears nowhere else. The two routines are back to back; matched code resumes at $0B4E (InitHW), and $092B–$0B4D is uncharted. A small symmetric pair with one MVN each is a recognizable shape: if another turns up, it is probably a save/restore pair for a different workspace.

docs.title: The entity dispatchers
docs.text:
The scene path left three callees: Sub_595C (33 bytes), Sub_597D (92 bytes) and Sub_E12A. The first two have no external calls; they only dispatch through an indirect jump table at $5D6E.

Sub_595C ($C0:595C–$597C, 33 bytes), called from Sub_01A5 once per scene load, walks the entity list:

  1. In 16-bit A, STZ $6D clears dp $6D and $6E in one instruction: the sprite-slot counter and the sprite-update flag.
  2. Load a 16-bit base pointer from $7F:2003 into X.
  3. Loop: load the entity type from $7F:2001,X; stop on zero. Otherwise save X to Y, compute type × 2, load the handler from ($5D6E + type×2), JSR to it, repeat.

Before the JSR the entity pointer is in Y; after it, the loop reads $7F:2001,X with the current X. So each handler must return with X pointing at the next entity.

Sub_597D ($C0:597D–$59D8, 92 bytes), called from Sub_1A03 once per active sprite slot (slot index in dp $6D), does the same for one slot's sub-list, found at $7F:2001 + slot×16 (four ASLs in 16-bit mode). After the terminator it:

  • steps X past the terminator and stores the pointer at $1180 + slot, recording where the slot's list ends
  • zeroes one 16-bit entry for the slot in each of eight arrays at $7F:0580, $7F:0600, $7F:0680, $7F:0700, $7F:0780, $7F:0800, $7F:0880 and $7F:0900 (stride $0080: eight parallel attribute tables)
  • stores $07 (three flags set) at $1C00 + slot, perhaps a "slot ready" or type-flags start state; not clear yet

The $5D6E table. Both functions use it. The first words are $5F74, $5F6E, $5FB6, $607E, ...: pointers to entity-type handlers in bank $C0, at least 30 before the first value that isn't obviously code. They are a future frontier. make diff was clean on the first pass; both org blocks went after Sub_1A03's RTS, and the two JSR $595C and seven JSR $597D call sites now use the labels.

docs.title: Sub_E12A: the sprite init pass
docs.text:
The first look at Sub_E12A reported "829+ instructions". That was the whole reachable subgraph. Its own body ends at the first RTS, at $E533: 1,034 bytes, $E12A–$E533. Its only two external calls go to $E534 and $E687, right after it:

  • $E534 ends at $E686 (341 bytes) and calls $E739, $E7BC, $E83F and $E8C2, each about 131 bytes, each a tight copy loop from a different ROM bank into WRAM.
  • $E687 ends at $E738 (178 bytes) and dispatches through internal jump targets.

In all, about 2,370 bytes in seven routines from $E12A to $E934 (1,034 own body + ~1,336 callee cluster). I deferred it, matched the entity dispatchers, and then came back to it the same evening as the head of its own arc.

It runs once per sprite slot during scene load, called from Sub_01A5 when dp $AE holds a valid slot. Four phases:

  1. Pointers. Builds two indirect-long pointers from four descriptor arrays ($1200, $1280, $1300, $1380, indexed by slot): [$CD] into $7F:XXXX, the sprite-data table (palette source), and [$D3] into bank($D5):XXXX, the scene-data table (tile layout source). $0D80+slot gets $3800 (the WRAM staging base), dp $D0 tracks the running WRAM write address, and $0F01+slot is cleared (a sprite-state flag). Early instructions set $D2=$7F and write $2181 (WMADDL).
  2. The 96-entry WRAM fill. After setting $2183=$01 and $2181=$3800, it reads 96 16-bit words from [$D3]+Y (Y from 0, two bytes per pass). Bit 14 picks the path: clear → JSR Sub_E687 (one WMDATA write), set → JSR Sub_E534 (multi-tile fill). The inner loop at $E173 does this test against $4000. The callee writes what it needs at the current address, and $D0 advances by $0020 on every pass except the first.
  3. DMA to VRAM. Channel 7: source $7F:3800, size $0C00, destination VRAM word $0400, port $2118 (VMDATA, BBAD7=$18), mode DMAP7=$01 (CPU→PPU, word increment), VMAIN=$80. It programs $4370–$4375 and triggers MDMAEN, copying 3,072 bytes.
  4. OAM staging. About 800 bytes. A lookup from $1700+slot gives an offset into $7F:4BC0, and the code fills 24 groups of 8 bytes (stride $08, bases $4BC2, $4BCA, $4BD2, …, $4C7A). Each group gets, from [$D3]+$C0 on: +0 a signed 8-bit value, +1 its sign extension ($FF or $00, via BPL / LDA #$FF / BRA / LDA #$00, 24 times), +2 a raw 8-bit value. Y walks $C0 to $EF. Then two constant passes: tile indexes at +4 ($40, $42, …$4E for groups 1–8, $60, $62, …$6E for 9–16, $80, $82, …$8E for 17–24, as 24 LDA #$xx / STA.l $7F4BCn,X pairs) and attribute $22 at +5 (one LDA #$22 and 24 STAs). $22 = %00100010: in the sprite renderer's attribute format, bit 5 is priority and bits 1–0 the palette, so priority 1 and palette 2.

It is big because it is fully unrolled: the 24-group fill alone is 24 × ~14 bytes = ~336 bytes. It runs once per slot at scene load, and on a 2.68 MHz CPU the loop overhead over 24 iterations is not trivial, so speed won over size. make diff passed on the first assembly; the local labels (.sp01–.sp24, .se01–.se24, .next_iter, .first_iter, .big_fill, .dma) resolved cleanly.

docs.title: 9 August 2026: the Sub_E12A cluster closes, and the slot allocators
docs.text: All six callees of Sub_E12A are matched in one pass, which completes the sprite init arc. Then the three sprite-slot allocators that sit just before it: 1,169 new bytes in 9 functions (sessions 26 and 27).

docs.title: What the cluster does
docs.text:
Sub_E12A runs the 96-entry WRAM fill behind the sprite-init DMA. On each pass it checks bit 14 of the scene word:

  • set → JSR Sub_E534: reads 32 bytes through a lookup table at $FD:0000 and streams them to WRAM via WMDATA
  • clear → JSR Sub_E687: works out which bank holds the tile data and copies 64 bytes (32 tiles × 2 bytes) straight to the WRAM address

Sub_E687 then tail-calls one of four bank-copy stubs, chosen by a bank ID in dp $CF.

docs.title: Sub_E534: the $FD00 table path
docs.text: Sub_E534 ($E534–$E686, 339 bytes; the earlier estimate was 341) extracts a byte index from the scene word, reads 32 bytes through the $FD:0000 table, and writes each to $2180 (WMDATA). It is fully unrolled: 32 blocks of LDA [$CD],Y / TAX / LDA $FD00,X / STA $2180 / INY, no loop, like the sprite renderer. It enters in 16-bit A (from Sub_E12A's exit state), switches to 8-bit for the 32 writes, and restores 16-bit before returning.

docs.title: Sub_E687: the bank dispatch
docs.text:
Sub_E687 ($E687–$E738, 178 bytes) computes an offset into the tile-data bank and dispatches on dp $CF:

$CF value Target Bank $7F Sub_E8C2 $7F (local via DB=$7F) $D2 Sub_E7BC $D2 $D3 Sub_E83F $D3 $D4 Sub_E739 $D4 $D5 inline .d5copy $D5

It uses CMP + BNE + BRL chains, because the stubs are more than 128 bytes away. Each BRL is a tail call: the stub's RTS returns to Sub_E687's caller. With no JSR/RTS pair, the stubs had to be in scope in the same pass.

Sub_E8C2, the $7F stub, differs from the others in one way: it uses LDA.w $0000,X (opcode BD, absolute indexed) instead of LDA $7F0000,X (opcode BF, long indexed). It has already set DB = $7F with PLB, so the absolute load reads $7F:0000+X and the long form would waste a byte. LDA.w stops asar from upgrading it to long.

docs.title: The db $A9,$7F trick
docs.text:
Each stub starts PHB / LDA #$7F / PHA / PLB. In the ROM, LDA #$7F at $E739 is the 2-byte 8-bit form, A9 7F. But in the source the stubs follow Sub_E687, which contains a SEP #$20 early (for the CMP against $CF) and a REP #$20 in the inline .d5copy path. By the stubs, asar tracks M=0, and LDA #$7F would assemble as A9 7F 00, three bytes. The fix is db $A9,$7F, which emits the two bytes regardless of mode.

The quirk can cost an hour the first time. In 16-bit mode asar zero-extends the immediate, but the ROM sometimes has the two-byte form, with the next byte being the next instruction. It wasn't in asar Quirks, so the first commit of session 27 added it there, next to the BRL offset quirk and the STA-with-equate quirk:

65C816 Assembly
db $A9,$7F    ; two bytes, exactly

docs.title: One set of bytes, two meanings
docs.text:
Sub_E534 and Sub_E687 share a header sequence. The ROM bytes at $E534 are:

Text Only
29 FF 07 0A 0A 0A 0A 0A 84 C5

With M=1 (Sub_E534's entry state): AND #$FF / ORA [$0A] / ASL / ASL / ASL / ASL / STY $C5, 10 bytes. With M=0 (Sub_E687's entry state): AND #$07FF / ASL / ASL / ASL / ASL / ASL / STY $C5, also 10 bytes.

The same bytes are correct for both call paths: Sub_E534 multiplies by 16, Sub_E687 by 32 (the extra ASL in M=0 supplies the factor of 2 that the M=1 path gets from the ORA). It looks like a deliberate encoding choice. So Sub_E534 is written in M=1 encoding (its real entry state from Sub_E12A) and Sub_E687 in M=0, and both emit 29 FF 07 0A 0A 0A 0A 0A 84 C5. The diff proved it.

docs.title: Who calls Sub_E12A
docs.text:
A raw byte search for JSR $E12A (20 2A E1) found exactly two call sites in bank $C0:

  • $C0:0212, inside the already-matched Sub_01A5. The main path: after Sub_595C dispatches the entity types, it reads dp $AE, and if the slot index is non-negative copies it to X and dp $6D and calls Sub_E12A.
  • $C0:47E9, inside an uncharted routine around $4700. The code checks $1201,X AND #$03 == $03 first, so this looks like a per-slot update path that re-runs sprite init for one flag combination. Noted, not matched.

Two callers fits a scene-load function, not a per-frame one.

docs.title: The slot-allocation trio
docs.text:
Between the matched Sub_E935 and Sub_E9E2, the range $E952–$E9E1 held three uncatalogued routines: the allocation counterparts to the deallocation routines Sub_E9E2/E9FF/EA1F.

The $0BC0 table holds up to eight one-byte slots. Sub_E935 sets all eight to $80, the "free" marker (bit 7 set, so a BPL skips it). Each allocator scans the table and claims the first free position:

Routine Size Searches Claims Sub_E952 40 B $0BC0[0..3] single $0BC0[X] Sub_E97A 48 B $0BC0/$0BC1[0..2] pair $0BC0[X],$0BC1[X] Sub_E9AA 56 B $0BC0/$0BC1/$0BC2[0..1] triple $0BC0[X],$0BC1[X],$0BC2[X]

All three share a post-claim body: turn the table index X into a WRAM staging base ($3800 + X × $0200) and store it at $0D80+slot. Carry signals the result: SEC for success, CLC for failure.

Sub_E97A stops at CPX #$03 (positions 0–2), not #$04. Pair positions overlap: position 0 claims ($0BC0, $0BC1) and position 1 claims ($0BC1, $0BC2). A position 3 would claim $0BC3 and $0BC4, the bytes the triple variant uses. Each variant's search range keeps different sprite types from colliding. All three match byte-exact.

Their callers ($CC0D, $CF2D, $D299, $D555, $D617) are all in the uncharted $CC00–$D600 range. My reading at the end of the day was that this range is a per-entity-type init layer above Sub_E12A: it calls the allocators, sets up the hardware multiply for WRAM offsets, then calls Sub_E12A or its kin. (The next day showed the call chain was not quite like that.)

docs.title: 10 August 2026: the animation-frame gate
docs.text: One routine today, Sub_CB3A (162 bytes), the gate at the start of every sprite-slot init routine. Scoping around it corrected yesterday's picture of the call chain and mapped a new cluster at $CB3A–$D800.

docs.title: Correcting yesterday's call chain
docs.text:
The goal was to scope the routines at $CF2D, $D299, $D555 and $D617 that call the slot allocators, and the $47xx code with its JSR Sub_E12A at $C0:47E9. Scoping showed the call chain from session 27 was backwards. Those four routines are not callers of a $47xx midlayer. They are sprite-slot init bodies that call Sub_E97A/Sub_E9AA directly, and nothing in $CC00–$D800 calls the $47xx code at all. The two are independent.

The bytes were always fine; every make diff passed. The mistake was in the prose: I had sketched a call graph from cross-reference data without checking the bytes at each address. The assembler enforces bytes, not descriptions, so the lesson is to check the disassembly before writing about who calls what.

docs.title: The sprite-slot init cluster
docs.text:
$C0:CB3A–$D800 (about 2,000+ bytes, 8+ routines) is a family of sprite-slot init routines with a shared template:

  1. Gate. LDA $1780,X; CMP #$03; BNE: for entity type $03, skip the gate and use $1301,X directly. Otherwise JSR Sub_CB3A; if it returns CLC, exit.
  2. Same-frame check. Compare the frame byte from Sub_CB3A with $0F01,X (the frame type loaded now). If equal, the sprite is already set up: CLC+RTS with no new allocation.
  3. Slot allocation. JSR Sub_E952, Sub_E97A or Sub_E9AA (1, 2 or 3 slots) by sprite type.
  4. DMA tile loop. Read the frame-data table via [$D3],Y; for each 16-bit entry, BIT #$4000: set → JSR Sub_E534 ($FD00-table fill), clear → JSR Sub_E687 (bank-switched tile copy). 16 or 32 passes.
  5. OAM staging. Write frame attributes (tile base, size bits, position offsets) to the $7F:48XX,X staging buffer.
  6. Finish. INC $1B00,X (mark the slot active); RTS.

All the callees (Sub_CB3A, Sub_E952, Sub_E97A, Sub_E9AA, Sub_E534, Sub_E687) are now matched.

docs.title: Sub_CB3A: the animation-frame gate
docs.text:
Sub_CB3A at $CB3A–$CBDB (162 bytes) is the shared first step. It computes dp $D6, a pointer into a frame-data table in bank $E4, from three entity fields:

$1600,X value Formula for $D6 0 $1500,X (base offset only) 2 2 × $1480,X + $1500,X > 0 (not 2) 3 × $1480,X + $1500,X < 0 (bit 7 set) $1480,X + $1500,X

It then adds animType × 4 + animRowHi to reach the current frame row, and reads the frame byte at [$D6]:

  • not $FF: SEC + RTS, the caller goes ahead with init
  • $FF, type 2: decrement the timer at $7F0B01,X. Still counting: CLC + RTS (skip this frame). Zero: also CLC + RTS (the caller handles the transition)
  • $FF, other type: wind $D6 back by animRowHi to the row start, store $FF to $1681,X (row finished), re-read the wrapped frame byte, SEC + RTS

The type 2 branch uses $1781,X instead of $1680,X as the column multiplier: a two-speed animation rate driven by the $7F0B01,X countdown.

Matching notes. There are no BRLs; every branch is in 8-bit range.

  • AND #$00FF / CMP #$0002 in M=0 need explicit 16-bit immediates.
  • LDA [$D6] assembles as opcode $A7 (dp indirect long).
  • LDA $7F0B01,X / STA $7F0B01,X are long indexed ($BF/$9F); asar uses long mode when the bank byte is explicit.
  • STA $D6, LDA $D6, SBC $D9, ADC $D9 and ADC $D6 use raw hex direct-page addresses, which avoids the equate-name quirk that forces long mode.

docs.title: 11 August 2026: the sprite-slot cluster takes shape, and an honest progress number
docs.text: Five body routines of the sprite-slot init cluster are matched, then the triple-slot dispatch. In between, the progress number gets a real denominator: matched code against the game's code, not against the whole 4 MB ROM. 2,377 new bytes in 7 functions (sessions 29 and 30).

docs.title: A word on yesterday's correction
docs.text: Session 27's notes made it sound as if routines like $CF2D and $D299 went through a "midlayer" around $47xx before calling the slot allocators. Disassembling them showed they call Sub_E97A directly; the $47xx block is a separate, unrelated region. I had sketched a call graph from cross-reference data without checking the bytes at each address. Corrections like this are cheap, because make diff enforces the bytes and a wrong description of who calls what can't corrupt the output. The discipline is to check the disassembly before writing prose about call graphs.

docs.title: The template, confirmed
docs.text:
Yesterday's scoping described a template: gate → same-frame check → allocate slots → tile-data pointer → DMA loop → OAM write → return. Matching five routines showed it is real. The routines differ in:

  • how many slots: one (Sub_E952), two (Sub_E97A) or three (Sub_E9AA)
  • whether the animation gate runs: Sub_CBDC calls Sub_CB3A; Sub_CDC8 doesn't
  • tile count and stride: 16 tiles × $28, 16 tiles × $50, or 32 tiles × $50
  • the starting Y offset in the tile data: $00 for the first pass, $20 for the second
  • which OAM staging buffer: $7F:4802+slot or $7F:4BC2+slot
  • what goes into $1B00,X: INC, INC twice, or set to $80
  • the return carry: SEC on first-pass success, CLC on OAM-only or second-pass

Once you see the template, each routine is a checklist. The differences are often a single byte: a multiply constant, a Y start, an OAM base address.

docs.title: Sub_CBDC: single slot, gated, 16 tiles
docs.text:
Sub_CBDC ($CBDC–$CDC7, 492 bytes) calls Sub_CB3A first, unless $1780,X == $03, in which case it reads the frame byte straight from $1301,X. If the gate passes and the frame is new, it claims one VRAM slot with Sub_E952, runs a 16-pass DMA loop with multiplier $28 (40 bytes per frame), writes four tile entries to $7F:4802+slot, and ends with CLC.

One detail: after STA $D9 (the palette-and-priority value), A still holds that value, and the first ORA $0C00,Y uses it directly. My first draft had an extra LDA $D9; the diff caught it.

docs.title: Sub_CDC8: OAM only
docs.text: Sub_CDC8 ($CDC8–$CEF4, 301 bytes) is the simplest: no gate, no slot allocation, no DMA loop. It computes the tile-data pointer from $0F01,X × $28 + $1380,X, loads the OAM slot index from $1700,X, and writes four Y entries (with sign extension into the high byte) and four X entries (entity base plus 2-step increments) to $7F:4BC2+slot. Then $1B00,X = $80 and CLC. It updates screen positions for entities whose tiles are already loaded, a light pass after the heavy init routines.

docs.title: Sub_CEF5: the three-way dispatch
docs.text:
Sub_CEF5 ($CEF5–$D123, 559 bytes; scoping had guessed ~660 for $CEF5–$D289) loads tile-table pointers in its header ($CEF5–$CF20) and checks $1780,X:

  • $1780,X == $03: a full 32-tile dual-slot init inline ($CF21–$D123). It allocates two slots with Sub_E97A, runs 32 passes (multiplier $50), writes eight OAM entries starting at tile-data offset Y=$40, increments $1B00,X twice (at $D11A and $D11D) and returns CLC. The double increment records that both halves loaded in one call.
  • otherwise, check $1B00,X & $7F. Zero (first pass): BRL $0369 to Sub_D28A. Non-zero (second pass or later): BRL $03EF to Sub_D30D.

Both BRLs are tail calls; the target's RTS returns to Sub_CEF5's caller. They need raw offsets because asar's BRL takes a literal displacement when the target is in another org block; see asar Quirks.

docs.title: Sub_D28A and Sub_D30D: a load split across two frames
docs.text:
Sub_D28A ($D28A–$D30C, 131 bytes) is the first-pass dual-slot routine. It calls Sub_CB3A, compares the frame byte with $0F01,X, allocates two slots with Sub_E97A, and runs a 16-pass tile loop from Y=0 with multiplier $50 to VRAM base $0D80,X. On success it increments $1B00,X and returns SEC.

Sub_D30D ($D30D–$D4F6, 490 bytes; scoping had guessed ~569) is the second pass. No gate, no allocation: it reuses what Sub_D28A set up on the previous frame. It uses VRAM base + $0200 for the second slot, starts the tile loop at Y=$20 (the second half of the 32-tile frame), and writes eight OAM entries from tile-data offset Y=$40. Then it increments $1B00,X and returns CLC.

So Sub_CEF5 runs once per frame. First call ($1B00,X & $7F == 0): Sub_D28A loads tiles 0–15 and returns SEC. Second call (== 1): Sub_D30D loads tiles 16–31 and returns CLC. The pass counter in $1B00,X tracks which half is pending. Sub_D30D is much longer because it has the eight-entry OAM block that Sub_D28A leaves to it.

docs.title: The denominator problem
docs.text:
I had been quoting progress like "0.38% of the ROM". That is true and misleading: most of a 4 MB SNES RPG is character sprites, tilesets, enemy graphics, maps, battle backgrounds, music samples and compressed audio, not code.

So I scanned the dscotton reference disassembly. Each bank file pulls raw asset data in with incbin. Summing those ranges and subtracting from each bank's 65,536 bytes gives the code per bank:

  • ROM total: 4,194,304 bytes
  • Asset data (incbin): ~3,835,026 bytes (91.4%)
  • 65816 code: ~359,278 bytes (8.6%)

Against 359,278 instead of 4,194,304, the 16,460 matched bytes are 4.6%, not 0.38%. Bank $C0 has 61,779 bytes of code, so 15,989 matched there is 25.9%, a quarter of the bank.

The breakdown also shows which banks are worth targeting:

  • $C1 and $CB are 97% and 94% code, nearly as dense as $C0: the obvious next big targets.
  • $C2 is 84% code.
  • $CA, $CC and $FD mix significant code with data.
  • $C4, $C5, $C8, $C9, $D0 and most of $D2–$EF are pure asset banks, 0% code. No point disassembling them.

The full per-bank density table is on the Bank Map page.

docs.title: Triple-slot dispatch: Sub_D4F7 and Sub_D608
docs.text:
The two "triple-slot stubs" from yesterday's table were estimates. Disassembling at $C0:D546 showed more structure. The code at $D4F7 is a dispatch routine, the triple-slot counterpart of Sub_CEF5. It:

  1. sets up graphics-bank parameters ($CF, $D2, $CD, $D8)
  2. bails at once for type 3 sprites, like the rest of the cluster
  3. reads $1B00,X & $7F, the pass counter
  4. checks whether $0D00,X equals $68, a sprite-size flag that picks between two load strategies

The paths:

  • Pass 0, not $68: falls through to Sub_D546 in the same body: two 8-tile DMA loops, to the WRAM slot base and base + $0200.
  • Pass 0, $68: BRL to Sub_D608, one 16-tile loop to the WRAM base.
  • Pass 1, not $68: BRL to Sub_D68B (unmatched).
  • Pass 1, $68: BRL to Sub_D738 (unmatched).
  • Pass 2+: two more BRL targets, unmatched.

Sub_D546 is reached by a short BRA, not a JSR, so it is an internal label. It is written as part of Sub_D4F7's body (273 bytes in all), with Sub_D546 kept as a global label for tracking. Sub_D608 is a real routine (131 bytes): animation gate, triple-slot allocator, 16-tile DMA, pass counter increment, SEC.

Both assembled cleanly, with a full 4,194,304-byte match on the first try.

docs.title: 12 August 2026: the sprite-init system closes, and a first look at bank C1
docs.text: The triple-slot routines, the dispatcher layer above the sprite-slot cluster and the animation queue that drives it are all matched, so the sprite system from $C98A to $E129 is one continuous run of matched code. Then a scouting pass over bank $C1, the battle engine. 3,509 new bytes in 10 functions (sessions 31 to 33).

docs.title: The last triple-slot routines
docs.text:
Yesterday left the pass-1 and pass-2+ tails of the triple-slot dispatch unmatched: four routines at $C0:D68B–$DD27, 1,693 bytes. Sub_D4F7 dispatches on a 2×2 grid: pass counter (1 vs 2+) × $0D00,X type ($68 vs not), each cell a BRL to its own routine.

Pass 1: Sub_D68B and Sub_D738. These are close to Sub_D608 (pass 0, $68), shifted in WRAM. Sub_D68B (not $68) loads WRAM slots at base + $0100 and base + $0300; Sub_D738 ($68) uses base + $0200 and base + $0400. Each runs two 8-tile DMA loops. They differ from the pass-2+ routines in two ways:

  • They reload LDX $6D at the top. The pass-2+ routines don't; they inherit X from Sub_D4F7, which still holds the entity slot. The raw bytes at $D7E5 settled it: C2 20 BD 80 0D, no A6 6D.
  • They end with SEP #$30 (A and X/Y both 8-bit before the INC/RTS). Pass 2+ uses SEP #$10: X/Y go 8-bit but A stays 16-bit for the OAM staging that follows.

Pass 1 exits INC $1B00,X; SEC; RTS: SEC means "not done, call me again".

Pass 2+: Sub_D7E5 and Sub_DA69. These also write the full OAM staging buffer: 12 Y entries with sign extension, the X entries, then attribute bytes. The sign-extension pattern:

65C816 Assembly
LDA [$D3],Y
STA $7F4BC2,X
BPL .pos
LDA #$FF
BRA .done
.pos:
LDA #$00
.done:
STA $7F4BC3,X   ; sign-extension byte

That pair of stores repeats 6 times, then come the X positions. Here the $68 difference shows: Sub_D7E5 (not $68) writes 8 X positions, then a CLC; ADC #$10 gap, then 4 more; Sub_DA69 ($68) writes 4, the gap, then 8. Different slot geometry for different sprite widths. The ADC #$10 is 69 10 (2 bytes) because A is 8-bit after SEP #$20, and asar's REP/SEP tracking got it right.

Pass 2+ exits INC $1B00,X; SEP #$10; CLC; RTS: CLC means "done". make diff: 4,194,304 bytes identical, once the SEP encoding and the LDX $6D asymmetry were right.

Text Only

  Sub_CBDC   $CBDC–$CDC7    492 B   Single-slot, gated 16-tile init

docs.title: The dispatcher layer
docs.text:
Scouting callers turned up the main sprite-init dispatcher at $CB0A–$CB30 and two more BRL targets: $D124–$D289 (~358 bytes, which I guessed was a single-slot OAM-only variant) and $DD28–$E129 (~1,026 bytes, a quad-slot or extended variant). All three are matched:

  • Sub_CB0A ($CB0A–$CB39, 48 bytes): the top-level sprite-type dispatcher
  • Sub_D124 ($D124–$D289, 358 bytes): an 8-slot OAM-staging initializer (type 1)
  • Sub_DD28 ($DD28–$E129, 1,026 bytes): a 12-slot OAM-staging initializer (type 2)

docs.title: The whole sprite-init system
docs.text:
Sessions 28–32 matched 15 routines spanning $CB0A–$E129 (5,664 bytes). As a system:

Every visible entity (character, NPC, enemy) is a "sprite slot", and each slot uses one, two or three hardware OAM entries depending on how many tile groups its art needs. When an entity appears, the game must (1) upload its tile graphics from ROM to VRAM and (2) describe the OAM layout: which tiles, where, in what priority and palette.

The VRAM-DMA cluster ($CB3A–$DD27, 12 routines, sessions 28–31) moves tile data:

  1. Sub_CB3A, the animation-frame gate: if the frame hasn't changed since the last init, return CLC (skip).
  2. Allocate sprite slot(s) from the free list via Sub_E952/E97A/E9AA.
  3. DMA loop: for each 16×16 tile entry, branch on a flag bit to Sub_E687 (normal tile copy) or Sub_E534 (described in this session's notes as a flip-transformed copy), and send it to VRAM.
  4. Increment the pass counter ($1B00,X) and return SEC (call again for the next pass).

It varies along two axes: slot count (single Sub_CBDC; dual Sub_CEF5/D28A/D30D; triple Sub_D4F7/D608/D68B/D738/D7E5/DA69) and layout, where $0D00,X == $68 picks a "left-heavy" 8+4 or "right-heavy" 4+8 X-position pattern.

The OAM-staging dispatcher layer ($CB0A–$CB39 + $D124–$D289 + $DD28–$E129, sessions 28/32) does no DMA. Sub_CDC8 (matched yesterday) was the first hint. Sub_CB0A reads bits 0–1 of $1201,X (the entity's sprite type) and tail-calls one of three routines with BRL:

Value Target What it does 0 Sub_CDC8 1-group OAM staging 1 Sub_D124 8-group OAM staging 2 Sub_DD28 12-group OAM staging other CLC + RTS no-op

First it validates the entity and bails if the sprite state flag has bit 7 set, if $1A81,X is zero or negative, or if $0F00,X is zero. All four early exits branch backward to one shared RTS at $CB11 instead of using a second RTS later. You only notice from the raw offsets, which are all negative and all hit the same byte.

Sub_D124 and Sub_DD28 run later in the frame, after the tiles are uploaded, and refresh the OAM staging buffer from precomputed animation data:

  • Sub_D124 multiplies the frame number by $50 (80), reads 8 tile-index/attribute pairs from Y=$40, and writes 8 OAM groups at $7F:4BC2–$7F:4BFC (stride $08). It reads the OAM buffer index from WRAM at $001700,X (a long access to bank $00, not the ROM table at $C01700).
  • Sub_DD28 does the same for 12 groups ($7F:4BC2–$7F:4C1C), frame × $78 (120), starting at Y=$60. If $0D00,X == $68 it takes an alternate layout with the X gap after the 4th slot instead of the 8th. Both paths read the index from the ROM table at $C01700,X (absolute mode).

Throughout, each tile-index byte is followed by $00 or $FF (bit 7 of the index), the "tile number high bit" for 512-tile sprite banks.

docs.title: The animation queue: the last gap
docs.text:
One gap was left next to the sprite system: $C0:C98A–$CB09, 384 bytes between the six-tile renderer (ending $C0:C989) and Sub_CB0A. It holds three routines, the animation clock behind everything above.

Obj_AnimTickAndQueue ($C0:C98A, 236 bytes) is the per-frame animation tick, called once per sprite slot. It reads the countdown at $1601,X, decrements it, and returns until it hits zero. Then it arbitrates focus slots: dp $76, $77 and $78 hold the primary focus, secondary focus and a tertiary mode flag. The sprite type in $1100,X decides the path: type 0 competes for $76, types 1 and 2 for $77. A winner increments its column counter $1681,X. Then it builds an address into a bank $E4 frame table: the row (from $1680,X or $1781,X by mode) × 4, plus the slot's base pointer from $1580,X, plus the column. A non-zero byte there becomes the new timer. A zero byte (end of row) falls back to the row base for the timer and adjusts or zeroes the column counter depending on whether the slot's loop counter has run out. Each sprite slot animates at its own pace.

Field_ProcessAnimQueue ($C0:CA76, 99 bytes) is the VBlank-time partner, called once per frame from the VBlank handler. It bails if $09A0 is non-zero (this stops it running twice). Then it latches the scanline ($2137 SLHV, then $213D OPVCT) and checks it against a threshold in $6B: if $6B ≤ V < 240 it exits, too close to the active display. Otherwise it takes the focus chain ($76, $77) and calls Obj_BuildSpriteFrameStep for the current slot. If the step reports "done" (carry clear), the slot leaves the chain ($1081,X set to $80) and the next one loads. It re-latches the scanline on every pass, so if VBlank ends mid-loop it stops. Re-reading the hardware counter, instead of counting cycles in software, is how an SNES VBlank task stays time-safe.

Obj_BuildSpriteFrameStep ($C0:CAD9, 49 bytes) is called by Field_ProcessAnimQueue and by the map-load pass at $C0:B109. It checks $1100,X, $1A81,X and $0F00,X in turn (carry clear if any fails), reads bits 0–1 of $1201,X, and tail-calls with BRL:

  • type 0 → Sub_CBDC (single-slot frame builder; this session's notes call the other two 8-slot and 12-slot builders)
  • type 1 → Sub_CEF5
  • type 2 → Sub_D4F7

All three targets are already matched; they return carry set when a frame was produced. With this, $C98A to $E129 is contiguous matched code.

docs.title: Where bank C0 stands
docs.text:
With the dispatcher layer, bank $C0 reached 19,114 bytes (30.9% of 61,779), and with the animation queue 19,498 (31.6%). The biggest uncharted blocks:

  • $59D9–$B191: ~22,425 bytes, between Sub_597D (ends $59D8) and Sub_B192. Likely more entity management, game-mode setup or map traversal.
  • $2E1E–$595B: ~11,070 bytes, after ClearRAMDMA and before the entity dispatchers.

Smaller gaps remain near the E cluster ($EA42–$EC5F, ~542 bytes), probably close relatives of matched code.

docs.title: Scouting bank C1
docs.text:
Bank $C1 is 63,904 bytes of code with only 1,632 bytes of incbin data: 97% code, the densest bank in the ROM. The dscotton reference names 481 routines in it, so almost nothing is uncharted. It is one integrated system.

The field engine enters it through one JSL $C10000 (Battle_Main), a JMP.W to a bootstrap that sets up the battle NMI/IRQ handlers, starts the battle main loop, and chains to banks $CF, $CC and $CD for the frame-by-frame battle tick. Bank $C1 is the coordination layer: battle menu, battler panels, stat bars, number display, enemy spatial queries and battle-phase sequencing.

It opens with a six-stub JMP vector table ($C10000–$C10018) and a bootstrap/dispatch block ($C10019–$C10088). Those 137 bytes mix data (the incbin jump table for the service dispatcher) and JML stubs, which makes them messier to verify. Right after, at $C10089, is a tight cluster of math leaf routines:

  • Battle_Mul8 (29 bytes): 8×8 hardware multiply via $4202/$4203/$4216. Input $AD/$AE, output $AF.
  • Battle_MulAccum (48 bytes): multiply-accumulate on the same hardware, into a 32-bit result at $A9/$AA. Sets DB=0 for the register access.
  • Battle_Divide (54 bytes): 16÷8 hardware divide via $4204–$4206/$4214/$4216. Input $B1/$B2/$B3, quotient $B5, remainder $B7.
  • Shift helpers (18 bytes, six overlapping stubs): Battle_ShiftLeft7, ShiftLeft4 and ShiftLeft3 fall through into each other; Battle_ShiftRight6 to ShiftRight3 do the same.

They touch only the hardware math registers and a few direct-page temporaries, with no WRAM layout to understand: the cleanest possible way to open a new bank. After them comes BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits at $C1:011F (decimal formatting for damage numbers), then the BattleUI and BattleMenu code.

docs.title: 14 August 2026: opening bank C1, from the math helpers to the battle windows
docs.text: Bank $C1, the battle engine, is open. In one day it went from an empty file to 4,085 matched bytes: math and number formatting, the battle status bar and all its callees, the item and tech list renderers, and the per-frame window upkeep. 33 functions over sessions 34 to 40, plus a root-cause fix in the disassembler.

docs.title: Opening a new bank
docs.text:
The build runs asar in patch mode: it starts from the original ROM and overwrites only the ranges the source covers. Opening a bank means:

  1. creating asm/bankC1/bankC1.asm
  2. adding it to asm/main.asm
  3. checking that make diff still reports 4,194,304 bytes identical before writing any matched code

The third step is not optional. If the new file emits or changes bytes outside its range by accident, the diff shows it at once. The build was clean before any code went in.

CPU state on entry. In bank $C0 the boot sequence leaves native mode, M=1 (8-bit A), X=0 (16-bit X/Y), DP=$2100, DB=$00 and the stack at $06FF. Bank $C1 is entered from the field engine with JSL $C10000 (Battle_Main), which JMPs into a bootstrap chain. The math routines at $C1:0089 are leaves called from deep inside that system, and their code assumes:

  • M=1 on entry. Each uses REP #$20 when it needs 16-bit A (to read a product) and SEP #$20 after.
  • X=0 (16-bit X/Y). The shift stubs never touch X; the multiply/divide routines use it once (an LDX in Battle_MulAccum to read the result register into a 16-bit index).
  • DP=0. Direct-page accesses ($AD, $AE, $AF, $A5, $B1 and so on) reach WRAM $7E:00xx.

DB varies. Battle_Mul8 writes the multiply registers at $004202/$004203 with STA.l (4-byte long form), which works whatever DB is. Battle_MulAccum saves DB with PHB, sets DB=0 (TDC / PHA / PLB) and uses the shorter STA.w. Battle_Divide goes back to the long form. That reflects what each routine can assume about its callers, not carelessness.

docs.title: The hardware multiply and divide
docs.text:
The SNES CPU has math helpers at fixed addresses in the $4200 space.

Multiply ($4202–$4216):

  • write the 8-bit multiplicand to $4202 (WRMPYA)
  • write the 8-bit multiplier to $4203 (WRMPYB); this starts the multiply
  • wait at least 8 master cycles (2 NOPs are enough)
  • read the 16-bit result from $4216 (RDMPYL/H)

Divide ($4204–$4214):

  • write the 16-bit dividend to $4204 (WRDIVL) and $4205 (WRDIVH)
  • write the 8-bit divisor to $4206 (WRDIVB); this starts the divide
  • wait at least 16 master cycles; the game uses 6 NOPs, which is conservative and safe
  • read the 16-bit quotient from $4214 (RDDIVL/H) and the 16-bit remainder from $4216 (RDMPYL/H)

The remainder and the product share $4216. Which one is there depends on the last operation, which is why RDMPYL appears in both kinds of routine.

docs.title: The math routines
docs.text:
Battle_Mul8 ($C1:0089–$00A6, 30 bytes; scouting had said 29). Reads $AD and $AE, mirrors them to $77/$78 (temporary storage, probably for the caller), writes both to the multiply registers in long form, reads the product with REP #$20 around the read, stores it at $AF, restores M=1, returns. The two NOPs after WRMPYB are the timing guard.

Battle_MulAccum ($C1:00A7–$00D6, 48 bytes). Does two multiplies and adds both into a 32-bit total: set DB=0 (so STA.w $4202 works), multiply $A5 × $A7, then $A8 × $A7, and add the products into $A9/$AA (16-bit low, 16-bit high). REP #$21 before the final ADC clears both the M flag (16-bit A) and carry in one instruction, so no separate CLC. PHP/PLP around the second multiply keep the processor flags safe across the register writes.

Battle_Divide ($C1:00D7–$010C, 54 bytes). Writes $B1 to WRDIVL, $B2 to WRDIVH and $B3 to WRDIVB, waits six NOPs (nearly twice what the hardware needs, a cautious choice for emulators and edge-case timing), reads the quotient from $4214 and the remainder from $4216, stores them at $B5 and $B7. An INC/STZ pair on $A029 brackets the work, like a "divide unit busy" re-entrancy guard. Whether anything reads it is a question for later; it is matched as is.

Shift helpers ($C1:010D–$011E, 18 bytes). Two fall-through chains:

  • Left: Battle_ShiftLeft7 at $010D has four ASL A, falls into Battle_ShiftLeft4 (one more ASL at $0111), which falls into Battle_ShiftLeft3 (three ASL + RTS at $0112–$0115). From ShiftLeft7 that is eight shifts, from ShiftLeft4 five, from ShiftLeft3 three. The reference names count each entry point's own contribution to the chain, not the total. (Eight shifts = ×256, handy for indexing 256-byte tables.)
  • Right: the same with LSR A. Loc_C10116 at $0116 leads into Battle_ShiftRight6 at $0118, then ShiftRight5 ($0119), ShiftRight4 ($011A) and ShiftRight3 ($011B–$011E, three LSR + RTS).

In asar this is one org block with a label at each entry; labels emit no bytes. After these four routines the project crossed 20,000 bytes for the first time: 20,119 across 4 banks.

docs.title: Number display
docs.text:
A caller audit of the math helpers: Battle_Mul8 is called from 11 sites across the bank, Battle_MulAccum from 13, Battle_Divide from 13, the shift cluster from 3. Almost everything in the battle engine uses them: damage formulas, stat scaling, experience. The first caller of Battle_MulAccum is at $C1:021C, inside Battle_SinLookup, just past the shift cluster in address order. That set the path.

The three routines between the shift cluster and the sine lookup format numbers:

  • BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits ($C1:011F, 85 bytes) splits a 16-bit value in a WRAM slot into hundreds, tens and ones by repeated subtraction, not hardware division: subtract 100 in a loop to count hundreds, undo the overshoot, do the same with 10, and the ones digit is what's left. Each digit is looked up in a glyph table at $CCF903 (bank $CC) to get its font tile, and the results go to four consecutive WRAM slots. The thousands slot always gets $FF, a blank marker that BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros later reads as "suppress this leading zero".
  • Battle_DivTen9499 ($C1:0174, 53 bytes) is the tens-and-ones half of the same logic, for two-digit numbers. Same subtraction loop, same glyph table, no hundreds pass.
  • BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer ($C1:01A9, 80 bytes) copies a 16-character text buffer with MVN, then turns each character into a pair: a tile index in one buffer and a "plane" byte in a parallel buffer. $40–$68 get tile offset +$40 and plane $71; $69–$72 get +$17 and plane $72; $73 and up pass through with plane $FF. The plane byte tells the renderer which of two tilesets holds the glyph.

A new entry convention. These three enter with A already 16-bit (M=0), set by the caller. BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer starts with its own REP #$20 anyway. FormatNumberDigits and DivTen9499 rely on the caller's M=0 for their 3-byte immediates (E9 64 00 for SBC #$0064 and so on). asar 1.91 has no "assume M:16" directive, so those instructions are written as raw db bytes. Everything else around them (LDA.w, STA.w, branches, stack operations) doesn't depend on M. make diff was byte-exact on the first attempt.

docs.title: Trig and geometry
docs.text:
Battle_SinLookup ($C1:01F9, 41 bytes) computes sin(A) * $AE and returns the high byte of the product in $AA. It multiplies the angle by 4, wraps it to 0–1023 with AND #$03FF, and uses it as a byte index into a 512-entry sine table at $C0F900 in bank $C0. The table holds magnitudes only. For the second half of the cycle (indexes $0200–$03FF) the code negates the value with EOR #$FFFF plus 1 (16-bit two's complement). The result goes to $A7, $AE is copied to $A5, and Battle_MulAccum does the multiply. It is the first matched routine that calls another matched routine.

Calc_Delta16 ($C1:0222, 119 bytes) turns a 2D displacement into a direction angle. It takes signed 8-bit coordinate pairs, ($D3, $D5) for X and ($D4, $D6) for Y, subtracts them into signed 16-bit deltas (sign-extending with the borrow trick LDA #$00 / SBC #$00), takes absolute values by XOR-and-subtract, and mixes them into a table index, roughly (|ΔX| >> 3) + (|ΔY| & $FFF8) * 4, in $E2. That indexes a base direction byte at $C0F300. The sign bits of the high bytes ($D8 for ΔX, $DA for ΔY) pick one of four quadrant paths, which add or subtract $80 or negate the angle.

It has dead code, kept byte for byte: after computing $E2 it does ASL A / TAX (2 × $E2 into X), then immediately overwrites X with LDX $E2.

Bank $C1 conventions so far:

  • M=1 on entry for most routines
  • M=0 on entry for the number-display routines, set by the caller and noted in each routine's header comment
  • X=0 (16-bit X/Y) throughout; no matched routine changes it
  • DP=0: direct-page accesses reach $7E:00xx
  • DB varies: the math helpers use STA.l for hardware registers because DB is unknown; BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer and Battle_SinLookup inherit DB=$7E from their callers and use absolute accesses to $94xx WRAM
  • no RTL: all of these are JSRed from inside bank $C1

docs.title: BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame
docs.text:
BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame ($C1:0299–$C1:05A6, 782 bytes) rebuilds the whole status panel whenever the battle needs it: entering a fight, a change of active character, HP/MP changes. It doesn't just draw numbers; it rebuilds the entire tilemap buffer.

The status bar is not a separate hardware layer. It is a rectangle of the same BG layer that shows the battle. The buffer at $7E:0CC0 is 192 word pairs (384 bytes) of (tile index, attribute byte); the attribute byte holds palette, priority and flip bits, and a DMA copies the buffer to VRAM every frame. In this buffer $29 is the normal palette and $2D the bright/highlight palette used for low HP or the active character. The font tiles for 0–9 live in VRAM, so a digit is just a tile index, chosen through the table at $CCF903.

The routine:

  1. clears all 192 pairs to (tile $00, attribute $29) in a tight loop
  2. writes border tiles (the separators between HP and MP columns, small corner tiles and so on) at offsets that depend on BattleGaugeDisplayType at $7E:9F20 (0, 1 or 2, three UI layouts)
  3. for each of the three PC slots that is active:
    1. writes the 5-character battle name from $7E:9412 (per-slot start from a table at $CCF837) into two tilemap rows: the tile row and a copy 64 word pairs earlier (the palette row)
    2. reads CurHp and MaxHp (per-slot pointer from $CCF8ED), formats CurHp into three digit tiles with BattleMsg_FormatNumberDigits, blanks leading zeros with BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros, and writes them at a gauge-type offset. It sets a low-HP flag at $7E:A10F when CurHp ≤ MaxHp/8, which switches the digit attribute from $29 to $2D, the palette that gives the flashing red
    3. for gauge type 0 (the "full" layout) does the same for MaxHp
    4. formats CurMp with Battle_DivTen9499 and writes it at another offset
    5. for gauge types 1 and 2, appends TP/ATB gauge tiles ($5D/$5E) and calls BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar
  4. handles the enemy slots the same way for names (11 characters from $7E:ACBC)
  5. if the highlighted PC changed, updates the tracking variables and dispatches a column-attribute update

BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros ($C1:104E–$C1:106D, 32 bytes) is its helper.

The db $69 pattern. The routine runs mostly with 16-bit A and adds or subtracts small constants like #$000E or #$0040 to tilemap addresses. asar 1.91 sometimes emits the 2-byte M=1 form ($69 $0E) instead of the 3-byte M=0 form ($69 $0E $00), which shifts every byte after it. The fix is the one used for SBC #$0064: write the bytes.

65C816 Assembly
REP #$20
CLC
LDA.B $84
db $69,$0E,$00          ; ADC #$000E — explicit 3-byte M=0 encoding
TAY

It came up thirteen times in this one routine, every ADC/SBC with a 16-bit immediate in M=0, so it now has its own entry in ASAR_QUIRKS.md (quirk #4). The original compiler happily emitted 3-byte immediates in 16-bit mode even for small operands; asar tries to be clever about operand size and sometimes guesses wrong.

At this point bank $C1 stood at 1,342 of 63,904 bytes (2.10%).

docs.title: The callees
docs.text:
All four callees stubbed by BuildStatusBarFrame (BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar at $C106F0, BattleSys_SlotPanelRefresh at $C10785, BattleMenu_DrawReadyWindowEdges at $C1081E, BattleUI_SetPanelAttrColumn at $C108E8) are matched, plus one more:

BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar ($C1:06F0, 149 bytes) draws the ATB gauge, the bar that fills while you wait for your turn (a chime plays when it's full). It computes the fill with the hardware multiply/divide: current ATB shifted left 8 (×256), divided by the maximum, gives 0–255; shifted right 3 (÷8) that is 0–31, for a 32-unit strip. From that it writes full 8-wide block tiles ($6F), one partial tile ($67 + remainder) and background tiles ($67) for the rest. The attribute is $2D if there is any ATB and $29 if the gauge is empty, which is why an empty gauge looks dim and a filling one bright.

BattleSys_SlotPanelRefresh ($C1:0785, 153 bytes) redraws the panel behind one character's status when the active PC changes. It writes a 6-row × 7-column tile block from one of two tables: $CCFA41 for the "empty" panel and $CCFA6B for the "ready" indicator (the look when a character's ATB is full and they're waiting for input). The choice goes through a cascade: a panel-state flag at $95F1, per-slot presence flags, a timing/animation flag at $A117, whether the PC-change flag $A6DE equals 3, and whether this slot is the active PC. Outer loop 6 rows, inner loop 7 tiles with attribute $29, plus 64 (the row stride) between rows. No callees.

BattleMenu_DrawWindowEdgeStrip ($C1:0929, 52 bytes) copies one vertical strip of the command window border (the Fight / Magic / Item box) into its tilemap at $7E:0B40. The tiles come from $D159FC in bank $D1. dp $84 picks the side: zero is the left edge (14 bytes per row, $0E in the table index), non-zero the right edge (12 bytes per row, offset 2 with INX INX). 6 rows, +64 per row. It is the first matched routine to read bank $D1; until now data came from $CC (tables) or $7E (WRAM). Bank $D1 looks like the home of the window decoration graphics.

BattleUI_SetPanelAttrColumn ($C1:08E8, 65 bytes) updates the attribute column behind the active PC. It doubles the slot index in A and looks up the tilemap column from $CCFA29 (gauge types 0 and 2) or $CCFA23 (type 1), since the layouts place the columns differently. Then it writes $29 to 10 positions, a 5-row × 2-column block, with absolute indexed stores.

BattleMenu_DrawReadyWindowEdges ($C1:081E, 202 bytes) draws the full border. It checks the slot states $A6D9, $A6DA and $A6DB; for each present slot (non-negative state) it picks a column and calls BattleMenu_DrawWindowEdgeStrip. The columns depend on who is present: if slot 0 is absent, slot 1's strip shifts left; if slot 1 is absent, slot 2's does. The $84 flag alternates 0 (left) and 1 (right). Then it calls BattleUI_SetPanelAttrColumn for the active PC ($A6DD), increments a redraw flag at $A43F, and falls through into a sub-entry.

BattleUI_ClearActivePanelColumn (sub-entry at $C1:0872) is also called from $C10C6E, so it has its own label. It zeroes a 6-row × 2-column block for the current active slot ($95D5), and if the redraw flag is set, repaints four corner tiles ($60, $61, $62, $63) at the newly active PC ($A6DD): a small mark showing which character is acting.

With these, every callee of BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame is matched.

docs.title: BattleUI_UpdateNextPcPanel
docs.text:
BattleUI_UpdateNextPcPanel ($C1:05A7–$C1:06EF, 329 bytes) is the incremental partner of BuildStatusBarFrame. Instead of a full redraw, it advances a rotating pointer ($A6E0) to one "next" PC slot, formats its HP/MP digits, picks the low-HP attribute, and draws the ATB bars for all three slots.

The first 28 bytes are early exits:

Text Only
LDA $A6DB      ; slot 2 state
BMI .common    ; absent → still update counter
LDA $A09A      ; update-inhibit flag
BNE .common    ; inhibited → skip digit refresh
LDA $9F20      ; gauge display type
BEQ .common    ; type 0 → fixed layout, skip
DEC A          ; type 1 → 0 (falls through); type 2 → 1 (branches)
BNE .common    ; type 2 → skip
JMP .tp_gauges ; type 1 → skip to ATB-bar draw only

Only gauge type 1 (HP+MP) reaches the digit refresh; type 0 (HP+MaxHP+MP) and type 2 (HP+MP+TP) skip it. .common increments $A6E0, wraps at 3, and checks slot presence before the digit update. The HP path reuses the low-HP test:

Text Only
LDA $5E30,X    ; CurHP (16-bit, M=0)
STA $9499
BEQ .set_low_hp
LDA $5E32,X    ; MaxHP
JSR Battle_ShiftRight3   ; maxHP >> 3
CMP $9499
BEQ .check_a110          ; tied: check secondary gate
BCC .hp_ok               ; maxHP/8 < curHP: not low
; else fall through to .check_a110
LDA $A110
BEQ .hp_ok
.set_low_hp:
INC.w $A10F    ; set low-HP flag (16-bit INC while M=0)

HP is low when curHP == 0, or when curHP <= maxHP/8 and $A110 is non-zero. Low selects $2D, normal $29. For gauge type 0, three extra attribute bytes go to $0CC9,Y / $0CCB,Y / $0CCD,Y, the MaxHP digit columns that layout shows.

The MP digits sit +$10 from the HP base for type 0 (which has the MaxHP column first) and +$08 for types 1 and 2, two more 3-byte immediates:

65C816 Assembly
CLC
LDA.b $86            ; base Y (saved earlier)
db $69,$10,$00       ; ADC #$0010 (type 0 path)
TAY
BRA .mp_dest_done
...
CLC
LDA.b $86
db $69,$08,$00       ; ADC #$0008 (types 1/2 path)
.mp_dest_done:
TAY
JSR Battle_DivTen9499

The tail draws the ATB bars for all three slots. It is a global sub-entry, Battle_DrawHpBars at $06DB, because it can be called directly:

65C816 Assembly
Battle_DrawHpBars:
    STX.b $80       ; slot counter = 0 (16-bit X = 0 stored to $80/$81)
.gauge_loop:
    LDX.b $80       ; load slot (16-bit DP load)
    LDA $96F5,X     ; slot presence flag
    BEQ .next_slot
    JSR BattleUI_DrawSlotGaugeBar
.next_slot:
    INC.b $80       ; 8-bit DP increment (only increments $80, not $81)
    LDA.b $80
    CMP #$03
    BNE .gauge_loop

INC.b $80 (E6 80) only touches $80, so $81 stays 0 and the 16-bit LDX.b $80 gets {$00, slot}.

Two matching notes. A global label inside a routine starts a new local-label scope, so after Battle_DrawHpBars: the earlier JMP .done and BEQ .done couldn't see a .done: defined after it. The shared exit became the global label UpdateNpc_exit:. And there are six LDX.w #$0029 / LDX.w #$002D (3-byte forms, M=1 with 16-bit X), each followed by TXA to get the attribute into A for the STA $0CCx,Y writes.

docs.title: The disassembler's X-width bug, fixed
docs.text:
In the status-bar callees, tools/disasm.py read LDX #$000C (A2 0C 00, 3 bytes with 16-bit X) as LDX #$0C (2 bytes) followed by a 00, producing fake BRKs and phantom BRLs into the $31xx range. The reference disassembly and the raw bytes gave the right decoding. asar itself tracked X correctly from context, since no SEP #$10 ever runs in this cluster.

The root cause: trace() started every trace with CPUState(m=True, x=True, e=True), emulation mode with 8-bit everything. That was fine in bank $C0 (the reset vector starts in emulation mode, and routines there often set 8-bit X anyway). In bank $C1, routines are entered with 16-bit X and no routine in this region ever does SEP #$10, so the model was wrong for the whole bank. The first clear case was at $C1:0640, where A2 29 00 decoded as LDX #$29 plus a phantom BRK, with branch offsets shifted after it.

The fix: trace() now defaults to CPUState(m=True, x=False, e=False) (native mode, 8-bit A, 16-bit X/Y), with a new --state option to override it per call. Full-bank linear sweeps of banks below $C0 keep the emulation-mode default, since those do start in emulation mode. $C1:0640 A2 29 00 now shows as LDX #$0029.

docs.title: Rendering the item and tech lists
docs.text:
The range $C1:095D–$C1:0C2C (720 bytes, 8 routines) is the battle menu's list rendering, the code that builds the visible item list and tech list in the command window. It has two branches, items ($C1:095D–$C1:0A87) and techs ($C1:0A88–$C1:0C2C), with shared helpers at the bottom.

Names via MVN. The name strings live in ROM bank $CC, and the code copies them to WRAM with the block-move instruction. asar's syntax puts the destination bank first:

65C816 Assembly
MVN $7E,$CC

That copies from bank $CC (ROM) to bank $7E (WRAM). The count is in 16-bit A, the source in X, the destination in Y. Each step copies a byte, decrements A, and increments X and Y, until A wraps from $0000 to $FFFF. Ten bytes per name (LDA.w #$000A before the MVN). Then the raw text at $7E:94A0 goes to BattleMsg_ReencodeTextBuffer.

A one-byte bug that shifted everything. BattleMenu_RenderItemRow computes an offset into the item-name table:

65C816 Assembly
SBC.b $84               ; * 11 (subtract factor)
db $69,$5E,$0B          ; ADC #$0B5E (M=0 three-byte form)
TAX

My first draft had a CLC between the SBC and the ADC:

65C816 Assembly
SBC.b $84
CLC                     ; ← wrong
db $69,$5E,$0B
TAX

make diff reported 185 bytes different, starting at $C1:09BD, the low byte of the JMP target for the empty-slot branch. CLC ($18) is one byte, so it pushed CODE_JP_C10A87 (the empty-slot RTS) from $0A87 to $0A88, the JMP target's low byte went from $87 to $88, and everything after moved by one, into the neighboring routines too. The original has no CLC because the SBC leaves carry in the state the ADC relies on. Removing it gave MATCH: 4194304 bytes identical. A one-byte insertion is not an assembler error; it just assembles to the wrong bytes, which is why make diff must pass before any commit.

A dead RTS. BattleMenu_RenderTechRow ends with an unconditional JMP CODE_JP_C10C00, and the next byte, at $C1:0BB5, is $60 (RTS). Nothing jumps to $0BB5, so it can never run. The diff compares the whole ROM, so it is emitted explicitly:

65C816 Assembly
    JMP CODE_JP_C10C00
    db $60                  ; dead RTS — unreachable, byte-exact pad

STA to address zero. The null terminator after the MVN is written with:

65C816 Assembly
STA.w $0000,Y           ; null terminate the name buffer

Without .w, asar emits opcode $97, the 2-byte STA [$00],Y (direct-page indirect long), a very different instruction. .w forces absolute indexed, opcode $99, the 3-byte form in the ROM.

The CODE_JP_ labels. CODE_JP_C10A87, CODE_JP_C10BB6 and CODE_JP_C10C00 are entry points that sit inside other routines but are jumped to from several places. CODE_JP_C10A87 is the plain empty-slot RTS at the end of BattleMenu_RenderItemRow. CODE_JP_C10BB6 and CODE_JP_C10C00 blank the MP-cost digit slots and copy the formatted name into the tilemap planes; BattleMenu_RenderTechRow jumps to one or the other depending on whether the slot holds a real tech or a skip.

docs.title: Window upkeep: the battle menu comes alive
docs.text:
In battle, a "window" is a rectangle of tilemap: the command window at the bottom (Attack, Magic, Item and so on) and the tech window that opens over it, listing techniques with MP costs and a cursor. They are WRAM buffers copied to VRAM once per frame, not PPU hardware windows. These routines prepare the data; the copy happens in a separate VBlank DMA.

BattleMenu_UpdateWindows ($C1:0C2D, 28 bytes) runs every frame. It reads $95D5 (the active PC slot), calls JSL $CFFD9E (BattleFx_SetPtrA2FromTable, a cross-bank setup), and dispatches on the submenu type $95DB: 0 → main command window, 1 → tech window, anything else → return. It reads like a modern switch statement.

BattleMenu_UpdateMainWindow ($C1:0C49, 58 bytes) handles type 0. It compares the active PC $A6DD with last frame's $A6DF. If they differ, it reloads the command window map (BattleMenu_LoadCommandWindowMap) and rebuilds the whole status bar (BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame, matched earlier today). If not, it refreshes the panel strips and redraws the cursor column when a flag is set. Either way it ends with JSL $CFFD02 to queue the $0CC0 region for VRAM upload and INC $99E2 to mark pending display work. It calls BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame ($C10299), BattleUI_UpdateNextPcPanel ($C105A7) and BattleUI_ClearActivePanelColumn ($C10872), so this layer sits above the status-bar layer and drives it as needed.

BattleMenu_UpdateTechWindow ($C1:0C83, 471 bytes, the biggest of the group) handles type 1:

  1. Text. Calls BattleMenu_RenderTechListRows ($C10A88, matched earlier today) to fill a $180-byte buffer at $99E3 with tech names and MP digits.
  2. Copy. Copies that buffer into the tech window tilemap at $A6E1, stepping by 2 (tile, attribute).
  3. Border. A 6×9 loop from the $CCFA95 template to $A70B,Y: one border row per outer pass, 9 tiles per row. A 16-bit ADC #$002E moves to the next row (stride 46, written as db $69,$2E,$00).
  4. MP digits. For each PC with techs to show ($96F5/$96F6/$96F7 != 0), converts current MP to digit tiles with Battle_DivTen9499 and BattleMsg_BlankLeadingZeros and stores them at $A751/$A7D1/$A851. A PC with no techs gets $FF (blank).
  5. Cursor target. Reads the current PC's scroll position and cursor row and goes through $CCF38C and $9551 to find the battler slot the cursor points at. An empty slot ($FF) blanks the relevant cells. A real battler has seven bytes copied from its WRAM entry ($1A80–$1A86) to scratch at $9EE3–$9EE9, and its HP-range values turned into digits.

It falls straight into BattleMenu_DrawTechCursorRow ($C1:0E5A, 96 bytes), which clears the old cursor by writing $FF over all six rows' cursor tiles (through BattleMenu_ClearTechCursorTiles, $C1:0EBA, a 39-byte leaf), then draws the new cursor, tiles $60–$63, at the current row, unless targeting is active ($9609 != 0 hides it during multi-target selection). Then JSL $CD0027 updates the info panel with the selected tech's name or description, and JSL $CFFD36 queues the tech window for VRAM upload. Render, then update, then the VBlank DMA through a cross-bank JSL to bank $CF: a clean vertical chain.

BattleMenu_UpdateTechMpAvail ($C1:0EE1, 349 bytes) decides whether each tech row is bright (affordable, attribute $29) or grey (too expensive, $2D). It loops three times, once per row:

  • slot types $FC and $FD are special: check the party size instead of MP
  • otherwise, resolve the battler slot and check each PC's current MP against the cost fields at $1A83, $1A85 and $1A86
  • if everything is affordable, check that the slot is menu-ready (BattleSys_SlotMenuReadyPredicate, $C1:103E, 16 bytes) and not locked ($A0D1). If so, clear the grey flag in $1A82 and write $29 to 18 attribute positions in $A6E2 and $A722; if not, set the flag and write $2D

The affordability test is a 16-bit compare by subtraction in M=1, with $96/$97 holding one PC's MP as two bytes: SEC / LDA.b $96 / SBC.w $1A83,X / LDA.b $97 / SBC #$00 / BCC _L1001.

A shared exit, and label scope again. UpdateMainWindow and DrawTechCursorRow both JMP to one RTS byte at $C1:103D, and UpdateTechMpAvail falls through to it; it is labeled CODE_JP_C1103D. In asar 1.91 every global label resets the local (.dot) scope, and UpdateTechMpAvail has several global sub-labels inside it (CODE_JP_C10F28, CODE_C10F66_JMP, CODE_JP_C1100F, _L1001), so its internal branches use a family of global-style _ump_* labels.

BattleMenu_LoadCommandWindowMap ($C1:1C3A, 16 bytes) rounds out the group.

docs.text:

Session totals: 150, 378, 814, 621, 329, 720 and 1,073 bytes. make diff confirmed 4,194,304 identical bytes after each.

Bank $C1 by the end of each session: 150 bytes (0.2%), 528, 1,342 (2.10%), 1,963 (3.07%), 2,292 (3.59%; 17 matched regions, up from 16), 3,012 (4.71%) and 4,085 (6.39%) of 63,904.
