For comparison, all of bank $C0 matched so far (19,498 bytes) is about 31.6% of its bank; at today's start, bank $C1 looked like a multi-year project on its own.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Bank $C1 has three broad areas: math and number formatting ($C1:0089–$C1:02xx), BattleUI and BattleMenu ($C1:02xx–$C1:1xxx), and enemy logic, animation and phase control ($C1:1xxx–$C1:FFFF, including EnemyAI_SpatialService at $C1:2986, a fully documented, isolated routine in the reference). The next neighbor is BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL at $C1:10E3, the target of the entry vector at $C10012 (BattleSys_EntryVec12 in the dscotton reference): the dirty-flag gate that decides whether UpdateWindows runs at all. After it, the cursor-movement and input layer that starts around $C1:106E.

docs.title: 19 September 2026: the battle command menu, from dirty flag to committed action
docs.text: The biggest single day so far: 1,478 bytes in 22 routines, all in bank $C1's battle command menu. It now runs as matched code from the gate that decides whether to redraw the menu, through controller input and confirm, to the 8-byte action record the battle engine executes. This is the first stretch of session 41, worked in eight increments.

docs.title: The dirty-flag gate
docs.text:
The battle menu doesn't redraw every frame. It waits until something changes, then does one full pass. Two sibling routines gate that pass, both on the WRAM flag $993A:

Text Only
LDA $993A
BEQ <exit>
STZ $993A
STZ $E5
JSR BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler
JSR BattleMenu_UpdateWindows
JSR BattleMenu_ProcessInput
JSR BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay

If the flag is clear they return at once. If it is set they clear it and run the rebuild: pull the next ATB-ready battler into the queue, refresh the window contents (matched on 14 August), process controller input, redraw the cursor overlay.

They differ in how they are reached:

  • BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyL ($C1:10E3, 23 bytes) is in the bank's cross-bank entry-vector table. Other banks reach it with JSL $C10012, which JMPs within the bank to $C110E3 without touching the stack, so the routine must return with RTL to match the long call.
  • BattleMenu_RefreshIfDirtyAndTick ($C1:10FA, 27 bytes) is a plain JSR target, called from several places in the battle-phase state machine. It adds a cross-bank tick (JSL $CD0009) before an ordinary RTS.

Same logic, two calling conventions. Two near-identical routines are not necessarily duplicated code; they can serve call sites with different stack contracts.

Three of those callees weren't matched yet (BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler at $C1:1B67, BattleMenu_ProcessInput at $C1:1153 and BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay at $C1:17DD), so they went in as label stubs: an org line with a bare label and no bytes, the trick used earlier in bank $C0 for forward references. asar resolves the JSRs, and a later increment fills in the body at the same org.

BattleMenu_DrawCursorSprites ($C1:1115, 62 bytes) sits between the gate routines and ProcessInput. It builds the four OAM entries of the cursor that points at the selected command. The shape is a fixed 4-tile template in ROM ($CCF604–$CCF607); the position comes from per-slot coordinates at $1D0C/$1D23, indexed by the active PC. The attribute byte's palette bits are replaced from $9F46 each time, almost certainly what makes the cursor flash or change color. What drives that byte isn't traced yet.

docs.title: Reading the controller
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ProcessInput ($C1:1153, 142 bytes) reads two WRAM bytes, $EE and $EF. They are pad-edge bytes: a bit is set only on the frame a button goes from released to pressed, not while it is held. $EE holds buttons (confirm is $80), $EF the D-pad ($02 left, $08 up, $04 down, $01 right). The routine:

  • no active PC ($95D5 negative): return
  • target-select mode ($9609 != 0, you're aiming at a target): hand over to BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput
  • submenu type $95DB is the tech or item list: hand over to that list's input handler
  • otherwise, the main command menu: check left, up, down, right, confirm, in that order

Each branch ends in a JMP, not a fall-through, so only one fires per frame. If two D-pad bits were somehow set on the same frame, only the first checked (left) would act. The hardware makes that close to impossible, but the dispatch is exclusive, not layered.

Four small leaves:

  • BattleMenu_CycleActivePcPrev ($C1:11E1, 55 bytes) and BattleMenu_CycleActivePcNext ($C1:1218, 56 bytes), for left and right, decrement or increment the active-PC index $A6DD, wrapping across the party (0..2). They skip any slot whose $A6D9 entry is negative (fainted or unavailable) by repeating until they land on a valid one. Both carry the cursor row ($95DC) from the old slot to the new one, so switching characters keeps your place in the menu.
  • BattleMenu_CursorUp ($C1:1250, 20 bytes) and BattleMenu_CursorDown ($C1:1264, 23 bytes) move $95DC for the active PC, wrapping over the three rows, and set a redraw flag ($A43F) so the cursor sprite moves next frame.

A branch that probably never runs. Both cycle routines branch on $A0D4 right after finding the new slot. Clear (normal): copy the cursor row across. Set: read a per-PC default row from $9916 and write it to the old slot's $95DC (through Y instead of X), which looks backwards. The reference disassembly flags this path as unreachable in the shipped game, and the odd target fits: leftover logic from an earlier version. It is reproduced byte for byte. The goal is a ROM that reassembles identically, oddities included.

Two borrowed leaves. Battle_ZeroResultEE ($C1:179C, 5 bytes) is STZ $EE, STZ $EF, RTS: the shared exit for nearly every routine here, clearing both pad-edge bytes once the input is used. Battle_StopSfx ($C1:1B55, 18 bytes) plays (or, by its name, cancels) a sound on cursor moves and confirms by writing $1E00–$1E02 and calling JSL $C70004, exactly like Sub_1B90 in bank $C0. The audio-command protocol is the same across the engine.

The same increment closed a tooling gap: tools/progress.py --update-index now syncs mkdocs.yml's stats block and index.md's matched-regions table from PROGRESS.md, instead of both being hand-edited every session (which had already drifted more than once).

docs.title: Pressing confirm
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ConfirmCommand ($C1:127B, 33 bytes) reloads the active-PC pointer, reads that PC's cursor row (0, 1 or 2: Attack, Tech, Item) and tail-jumps to the matching handler. On the way it writes $FF to $A0D7. Nothing here reads it back, but the reference shows it compared inside BattleUI_BuildStatusBarFrame, so it is probably a marker that forces a status-bar refresh next time.

  • BattleMenu_ChooseAttack ($C1:129C, 32 bytes, row 0) sets the target mode $960D to $07, calls the target-list builder, and increments $9609, the flag ProcessInput checks first. Confirming Attack doesn't open a submenu. It changes what the next frame's input handler means.
  • BattleMenu_OpenTechList ($C1:12BC, 49 bytes, row 1) and BattleMenu_OpenItemList ($C1:12ED, 51 bytes, row 2) render their lists (with the routines matched on 14 August), set the submenu type $95DB and return. The item version also copies a fixed $180-byte graphic into the command-window tilemap. The reference calls it ItemBoxBattles, in bank $D1 next to the TechBoxBattles graphic that BattleMenu_LoadCommandWindowMap uses. Presumably the item list needs a different border. Both gate on a flag at $A0A7 that reads like "list locked"; what would lock it (a status effect? a command restriction?) isn't clear, so it is a loose end.

docs.title: Building the target list
docs.text:
BattleMenu_BuildTargetList ($C1:1F79, 100 bytes) is what ChooseAttack calls. According to the reference, the tech-confirm and item-confirm paths call it too, so it is a shared dependency for three submenus.

It resets a handful of target-selection variables and fills two 11-entry lists, candidates and selection, with $FF. Eleven fits the layout: 3 party members plus up to 8 enemies. If target-select isn't already active in a "return here on cancel" state, it saves the current submenu type to $A86B before clearing it, so cancelling brings you back to the menu you were in (main, tech or item) instead of the top.

Then it clamps the target mode $960D into range, doubles it into a word index and jumps through a table: JSR ($1FF8,X). Each entry is a handler that knows how to collect targets for one mode (Attack, an area tech, a party-wide heal...). That table and its dozen-plus handlers (BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets, BattleTgt_ListEnemiesSingle and others in the reference) are a separate subsystem. BuildTargetList refers to the table by raw address and stops there, the same deferral used for bank $C0's $5D6E entity table.

The bug. An early draft put LDA #$FF inside the clearing loop:

Text Only
; wrong
.clear_loop:
    LDA #$FF
    STA $99C0,X
    STA $A62D,X
    DEX
    BPL .clear_loop

The ROM loads it once, before:

Text Only
; correct
LDA #$FF
.clear_loop:
    STA $99C0,X
    STA $A62D,X
    DEX
    BPL .clear_loop

Both behave the same, but moving the load changes where the loop starts, so the BPL offset changes. make diff flagged one byte at $C1:1F9C, the offset byte. Byte-exact matching checks the encoding, not just the logic: a change any reviewer would call "obviously equivalent" still fails, at once.

docs.title: The ready queue
docs.text:
ATB means battlers act when their gauge fills, not in strict turns, so several can become ready in the same frame or while the menu is busy. BattleMenu_DequeueReadyBattler ($C1:1B67, 67 bytes) handles that with a 3-slot FIFO at WRAM $95D6-$95D9 and a count at $95DA. Dequeuing:

  • restores the battler's saved cursor row (if you left it on "Item", it's still on "Item")
  • marks the slot present in the active roster
  • shifts the remaining entries down one
  • if nobody is the active menu PC, makes this battler the active one

One line looks odd out of context: STA $A6D9,X with A and X both holding the slot's own index. Elsewhere today $A6D9,X is a presence check (BMI after loading it means "slot empty"). Writing the slot's index there is the "occupied" marker, not a translation table.

The shift reads $95D8 twice, writing it to $95D7 and then $95D9, instead of reading $95D9 for the second write. Since the count never exceeds 3, it probably never matters, and it is reproduced as is. This closed the last stub callee of the dirty-flag gate.

BattleMenu_RemoveBattlerFromReady ($C1:1BAA, 144 bytes), next door, is the inverse. A battler may be waiting in the queue or already promoted to the active menu character, and it tells them apart by $A6D9,X (negative: not promoted). From the queue it scans for the entry and shifts the rest down, starting anywhere, not just at the head. For the active PC it also has to leave the menu in a sane state:

  • cancel target selection ($9609 and a couple of related flags)
  • reset the submenu type to the main menu ($95DB)
  • clear the battler's roster slot
  • search the roster for another battler to promote, or explicitly set "no active PC" if there is none, so $A6DD/$95D5 never point at stale data

The same bug, again. An early draft put a one-time load (LDA $80, the slot to search for) inside the scan loop. make diff flagged one byte on the loop's closing branch, as with BuildTargetList. A lone one-byte diff on a branch operand near loop code is now my first guess.

docs.title: Target-select input
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput ($C1:1561, 185 bytes) reads the controller while you point at an enemy or ally. Unlike the main menu, it calls BattleMenu_BuildTargetList on every call, because valid targets can change mid-selection (an enemy can die from a status tick). If the rebuild finds no target, or you cancel, it leaves target-select and restores the previous menu (main, tech or item), repainting its window as needed. Otherwise it polls the pad: confirm tail-jumps to BattleMenu_CommitAction; the D-pad cycles forward or backward through targets, unless the mode targets everyone, which disables cycling.

Eighteen bytes that never run. In the middle of the cancel path is something shaped like a second copy of the item-window graphic loader: same source table, same destination. But its loop branch points forward, into the confirm/cycle section, not back to itself. If it ran it would copy one byte and leave, nowhere near the 384 bytes the working copy loop elsewhere in the routine moves. And nothing reaches it: every path before it ends in an unconditional branch past it. These are bytes the CPU can never execute under any input or game state. The single orphaned RTS on 14 August was the only dead code seen before; this is the first dead multi-instruction block. The likely story is a branch target changed during development and the old live code left behind. Either way, it is reproduced exactly.

docs.title: Committing the action
docs.text:
Every confirm press ends in BattleMenu_CommitAction ($C1:161A, 308 bytes), the largest routine in the command-menu cluster. It builds a uniform 8-byte record, "character X does Y to target Z", whether Y is an attack, a tech or an item. It dispatches on $95DB to fill in the parts that differ, then joins shared code that writes the record and hands off. Attack is almost trivial: a type flag and a marker for "no tech or item id". Item decrements the item's stock and clears some UI scroll state. Tech is the interesting one, because dual and triple techs involve more than one character.

BattleMenu_ConsumePartnerSlot ($C1:174E, 30 bytes) takes a combo partner out of the turn pool so it doesn't also act on its own later: it clears the slot's presence in the active roster (decrementing the active-PC count if it was on screen) and clears a flag bit on that battler's sprite data (called the "queued" bit at the time). CommitAction calls it once for a dual tech's partner (low nibble of $9EE7) and again for a second partner only if the high nibble says triple tech. The combo bookkeeping was built to scale from two to three, not bolted on.

Then the same cleanup seen in RemoveBattlerFromReady: clear the confirming character's slot, then find another active menu character or mark "no active PC".

BattleMenu_TargetNext ($C1:176C, 26 bytes) and BattleMenu_TargetPrev ($C1:1786, 22 bytes) move the target cursor through valid targets, skipping invalid slots, with the same wrap-and-retry shape as CycleActivePcPrev/Next. TargetPrev has no RTS of its own: it sits right before Battle_ZeroResultEE and runs into it.

With CommitAction, everything from the dirty-flag gate to a confirmed target is one unbroken span of matched code. Working a cluster in order pays off: callees stop being stubs one by one until the whole subsystem is visible.

docs.title: Fixing the progress bookkeeping
docs.text:
Before any code, the standing staleness audit (checking that PROGRESS.md's headline, its per-bank headings and the generated homepage snippet agree) found two real bugs. The bank $C0 heading had read 384 bytes low since session 33, when that session's total went in without updating it. And tools/progress.py choked on comma-formatted byte counts, so bank $C1 had been missing from the generated summary since it opened. Both are fixed: the heading corrected, and the parser strips commas before converting.

Right after the first routines, the same class of bug came back: the bank $C1 table got its new rows, but the heading's byte count didn't move until the audit ran again. Twice in one sitting means a process gap, not a slip; the fix belongs in tooling, which is what the --update-index change above does.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Two submenu-input stubs remain: BattleMenu_TechListInput and BattleMenu_ItemListInput, which mirror each other and TargetSelectInput. Behind them, per the reference, sit routines like BattleMenu_TechConfirm and an item-confirm equivalent. Also still open: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay ($C1:17DD), the 117-byte periodic/idle-check service at $C1:106E, and the target-mode handler table at $C1:1FF8, a dozen-plus BattleTgt_* handlers referenced only by address so far, which deserves a session of its own.

docs.title: 22 September 2026: the tech and item lists, and the command menu is closed
docs.text: The input handling for the tech list and the item list is matched, the last two submenus still holding stubs. Every input handler in the battle command menu is now matched code. 637 bytes in 15 routines, the last two increments of session 41.

docs.title: The tech list: one cursor, two coordinate systems
docs.text:
BattleMenu_TechListInput ($C1:1320, 73 bytes) runs every frame the tech list is open. It works out which entry is highlighted (scroll position plus cursor row), then checks the pad for confirm, cancel or a direction. BattleMenu_TechConfirm ($C1:1369, 38 bytes) hands over to targeting, like BattleMenu_ChooseAttack does for Attack. BattleMenu_TechListCancel ($C1:138F, 30 bytes) restores the cursor and scroll saved before the list opened and goes back to the main menu.

Not every tech in the list is selectable. A character may not have learned it, or may not have the MP. Those entries carry an availability flag, and the cursor must skip them. But two things are being tracked: the tech's index in the underlying list, and where the cursor sits on screen (a row 0–2 plus a scroll offset). Press up when the previous entry is unavailable, and the cursor has to move to the next available entry, which may be two or three list slots away.

BattleMenu_TechListPrev ($C1:13AD, 71 bytes) and BattleMenu_TechListNext ($C1:13F4, 73 bytes) solve it by counting. Each walks the list index one step at a time, checking the flag, until it reaches a selectable entry, and counts the steps. Then it replays that count on the screen position (row and scroll), scrolling the window by a row whenever the cursor would leave the visible part. Two loops, same shape, same count, applied to two representations of "where you are". The list walk finds out how far you moved; the screen replay trusts the number without needing to know why. The availability flags are only checked once.

docs.title: The item list: almost the tech list, but simpler
docs.text:
BattleMenu_ItemListInput ($C1:143D, 91 bytes) has the same confirm/cancel/up/down checks plus two branches the tech list lacks: page the list up or down three rows at once, and a check of a flag ($A0D0) that forces a full re-render when something elsewhere has marked the display stale.

Cursor movement is where it differs most. Items don't need skipping: an unusable item still gets a cursor position and just renders greyed out. So BattleMenu_ItemCursorUp ($C1:14EC, 22 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemCursorDown ($C1:1502, 26 bytes) move the row by one and only call a scroll helper at the top or bottom edge of the window. Same UI pattern, different implementation, because the two lists have different rules for where the cursor may stop.

Borrowing another routine's ending. BattleMenu_ItemListPageDown ($C1:151C, 27 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemListPageUp ($C1:1537, 20 bytes) don't call the renderer themselves. They set the scroll position and JSR into the middle of BattleMenu_ItemListScrollDown ($C1:17BF, 30 bytes) / BattleMenu_ItemListScrollUp ($C1:17A1, 30 bytes), right at the instruction that calls the renderer, so that routine's tail (render, then flag the scroll arrows for a refresh) does double duty. Bank $C0's Sub_1BA7 does the same, entering Sub_1B90 partway to reuse its tail. On the matching side, that internal entry point had to be a real global label instead of a private .dot label: in asar a new global label resets the local scope, so a label jumped to from outside must be global.

A branch that can't happen. BattleMenu_ItemListScrollUp opens with two BEQs in a row on the same flag, with nothing in between that changes it. The first is a normal check. The second asks a question already answered: if the flag were set, the first branch would have fired. This is a different kind of "does nothing" from the dead block in BattleMenu_TargetSelectInput three days ago. That was code nothing can execute; this runs every time and always gets "no". Both are reproduced exactly.

BattleMenu_ItemConfirm ($C1:1498, 67 bytes), BattleMenu_ItemListCancel ($C1:14DB, 17 bytes) and BattleMenu_ItemListRefresh ($C1:154B, 22 bytes) complete the set.

docs.title: Fixing an old label
docs.text: Working out an item record for ItemConfirm (id, target mode, flags, quantity, in that order, five bytes apart) showed that BattleMenu_RenderItemRow, matched on 14 August, had two field comments backwards: it called the quantity field "item ID" and the id field an "unconfirmed-animation flag". That routine only reads the fields; ItemConfirm's branches reveal what they mean. The old comments are corrected. No bytes changed.

docs.title: What this closes
docs.text: Every submenu the command window can open, the main Attack/Tech/Item menu, the tech list, the item list and target selection, now has matched input handling and confirm logic, and the tech and item lists have matched navigation. Together with the confirm dispatch and command commit from 19 September, the whole path from "the menu needs a redraw" to "a battle command has been built and queued" is byte-exact end to end.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay at $C1:17DD, the last single-routine stub in this neighborhood. After that, the target-mode handlers behind $C1:1FF8, and the much larger territory past $C1:1C4A: enemy logic, battle animation and most of the 481 routines scouted when the bank opened.

docs.title: 24 September 2026: the cursor that draws itself
docs.text: One big routine: BattleMenu_UpdateCursorOverlay, 828 bytes, the last stub in the command-menu neighborhood. Every frame, after input is processed, it decides what the pointing hand (or hands) on screen should look like, and where.

docs.title: One routine, four jobs
docs.text: It starts with dispatch. If no party member is choosing a command, hide the cursor and stop. If the player is picking a target, draw target cursors. Otherwise branch on the open submenu: main, tech or item. The main menu path does nothing: its cursor was already drawn earlier in the frame by BattleMenu_DrawCursorSprites, so it skips to the end. The other three paths each solve a different problem, so it reads like four small routines stitched together.

docs.title: Dual and triple techs get more than one hand
docs.text:
Combo techs need the cursor to show who is involved. The tech path checks the highlighted tech's id. Below $39 it is a single-character tech and gets one hand. At $39 and above, it reads a byte that packs the partners into two nibbles (low nibble first partner, high nibble second, $F meaning nobody) and places one cursor over the caster and one over each partner.

Every placement uses the same formula: the battler's base screen position, plus a second per-battler offset (probably the live animated position), minus 16 to center the sprite. It appears six times, unrolled each time instead of in a helper. On a 3.58 MHz CPU, saving a JSR/RTS per cursor was apparently worth the bytes.

docs.title: The item list only redraws when it has to
docs.text:
The item path manages the up/down scroll arrows and the row highlight, and keeps a cached copy of the last value drawn for each. If the live value matches the cache, nothing is touched. Only on a change does it redraw, and only then does it ask for the tile buffer to be uploaded to video memory.

At the top of the list the up arrow is hidden; at the bottom (scroll position $FA) the down arrow is hidden. When the down arrow is visible it uses attribute $A9 instead of the usual $29, unlike the up arrow. That looks deliberate: "more below" gets the emphasis, "more above" doesn't.

docs.title: Picking a target, and "target all"
docs.text:
Single-target selection draws one cursor over the chosen battler. Only in the plain Attack menu, and only when the target is an enemy, it goes through one of two cross-bank message calls that drive the enemy info panel. A per-enemy flag table at $E1DE80 decides whether the panel gets the real target id or $FF. Neither callee is matched yet, so their exact behavior is a guess.

Multi-target selection took the longest to understand. There are only four cursor sprites, but a "hit everything" tech can target more battlers than that. The routine doesn't draw them all in one frame. It scans the selection list three entries at a time, saves where it stopped ($960B), and continues from there next frame, wrapping to the start after six. The cursors alternate between groups of targets on successive frames: limited sprites, so the work and the drawing are spread across frames, a trade-off the SNES forces on many games.

docs.title: Matching notes
docs.text: Nothing exotic, but the size made bookkeeping matter. There are forty-two local .labels, all branch targets inside this one routine. Several branches are just out of 8-bit range, so the original uses a short branch to a nearby JMP. Those trampolines (.tech_single_jmp, .to_tail and others) have to sit exactly where they are, or every address after them shifts.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The command menu has no stubs left. The next piece is the target-mode handler table at $C1:1FF8, a dozen-plus BattleTgt_* routines the menu calls but that are only referenced by address so far. First a small gap: $C1:1B19–$C1:1B54, between this routine and Battle_StopSfx.

docs.title: 8 October 2026: who can you hit? The target modes
docs.text:
The code that answers "who does this action hit?" for the battle menu is matched: a 33-entry table of target modes and the eighteen small routines behind it, plus the routine that puts a character into the ready queue. 1,033 bytes in 26 functions (session 43).

Cyclone hits whoever is near the enemy you picked. Aura heals one ally. Luminaire hits everyone. Every action ends with that question, and this is the code that answers it.

docs.title: Joining the queue
docs.text:
BattleMenu_EnqueueReadyBattler ($C1:1B19–$C1:1B54, 60 bytes) is the opposite of DequeueReadyBattler from 19 September. Nothing in this bank calls it directly, which was confusing at first. The answer is the small service table at the top of the bank: other parts of the engine call $C10045 with a service number. Service 1 is this routine; service 2 is RemoveBattlerFromReady. So when a character's gauge fills, another bank asks the battle engine to queue them, and this runs.

It does four things:

  1. skips characters already in the active roster
  2. sets a "waiting for a command" bit on the character
  3. appends the character to the queue and resets their menu cursor to its default row
  4. plays a sound through the same audio command as Battle_StopSfx, with sound id $42, very likely the "turn ready" cue

That bit fixed an old mistake. ConsumePartnerSlot's comments called bit 7 of that flag byte the "queued" bit. Now that I can see what sets it, bit 7 means "waiting for a command", and bit 6 (set by CommitAction) means "command queued". The comments are corrected; no bytes changed.

docs.title: Thirty-three modes, eighteen routines
docs.text:
The target-mode table (BattleTgt_ModeTable, $C1:1FF8–$C1:2039) has 33 entries but only 18 distinct handlers, and 12 of the 33 point at the default "pick one ally" handler. That looks like room left for modes nobody needed.

The simple modes share one list builder. Each picks a slot range (allies 0–2, enemies 3–10), optionally sets "target everything", and jumps into BattleTgt_CollectValidTargets. It walks the range and keeps each battler that is present, not flagged out and not hidden. A battler marked KO'd only gets in when the mode is $04. If the caster is in range, they always go first, so when you heal, the cursor starts on yourself.

A few modes are more particular:

  • Self: just the active character. Three instructions.
  • KO'd ally: an unrolled check of each party member's status byte for the "down" bit. That is the revive target list.
  • A specific character: two modes search the party for one character id (4 and 5) and target only them. If that character isn't in the party or can't be targeted, the mode reports "no target". This is how a combo tech can insist on a particular partner.

docs.title: Area attacks
docs.text:
The other modes are area modes, and they share one recipe:

  1. Pick an anchor: the caster, an enemy you aim at, or a party member found by character id.
  2. Fill a small parameter block: source, aim point, a shape/size code and a variant flag.
  3. Call a geometry routine that works out who is inside the area.
  4. Select the whole result.

The enemy-anchored modes still let you move the cursor. Watching the pad bits shows a quirk: the three "line from the caster to the enemy" modes step the cursor forward whether you press left/up or right/down, while the other area modes step backward for one of the two. I don't know yet whether players ever notice.

The radius modes use two size codes, and one mode in each pair swaps in a bigger one ($19): two different techs sharing a handler, told apart by mode number.

The geometry routines (four of them, roughly 1.1 KB from $C1:2332) aren't matched yet. For now they are label stubs, so the handlers can call them by name.

docs.title: A second door into the same room
docs.text: BattleTgt_RunAreaQuery is service 7 in the same service table. It is a 13-byte dispatcher with its own 7-entry table pointing at the same four geometry routines ($C1:1FDD–$C1:1FF7 together). So the menu isn't the only thing asking "who is in this area?". Something outside the bank asks too, most likely enemy attacks, which need the same answer.

docs.title: Little things
docs.text:
• BattleTgt_CycleNext/CyclePrev duplicate the menu's TargetNext/TargetPrev (19 September) instead of sharing them.
  • BattleTgt_EnemyArea2332 has a dead RTS after its final JMP. Nothing reaches it, but it is in the ROM, so it is in the source.
  • BattleTgt_ClearLists blanks 12 entries of lists that only ever use 11.

docs.title: A better check
docs.text: Building on top of the original ROM has one blind spot: if a routine somehow didn't get written at all, the original bytes would still be there and make diff would report a match. So I also rebuilt over a copy of the ROM with every newly matched range zeroed first, and compared again. All 1,033 bytes came back from source.

docs.title: Boot
docs.text:
Power-on and reset. The 65C816 starts in emulation mode at the reset vector in bank $00, which switches to native mode and jumps to MainInit in bank $FD; MainInit sets up the CPU and the PPU and hands over to GameLoop. The NMI and IRQ vectors point at small stubs that jump to handlers installed in RAM.

See also: Bank Map, Architecture.
